Q5513.t: The deepest lake on Earth, a blue crescent in Siberia
Q5513.s: Look for a long blue crescent pressed between dark mountain ridges — that's Baikal, more than 600 km from end to end. Its deepest point is 1,642 m down, deeper than any other lake on Earth. In late winter the ice turns glassy and pale turquoise, split by cracks that run for kilometres.
Q5513.w: A narrow crescent of deep blue, or white ice in winter, running south-west to north-east between mountains.
f: Baikal holds roughly a fifth of all the unfrozen fresh water on Earth's surface.
More than 300 rivers flow into it, but only one — the Angara — flows out.
It is home to the nerpa, a seal that lives nowhere else in the world.

q.q: Which river is the only one flowing out of Lake Baikal?

Q23883.t: The lowest water on Earth, and it keeps sinking
Q23883.s: The shore of the Dead Sea is the lowest dry land on the planet, more than 430 m below sea level — and the water drops by roughly a metre a year. It is so salty that people float without trying. From above, the deep-blue northern basin gives way to pale geometric salt pans in the south.
Q23883.w: A slim blue lake in a deep desert trough east of Jerusalem, with turquoise and white salt ponds at its southern end.
f: Its water is roughly ten times saltier than the ocean — too salty for fish.
The Jordan River is its main source, and nothing flows out: water leaves only by evaporation.
The southern basin is now mostly a patchwork of evaporation ponds for potash and salt.

q.q: Roughly how far below sea level is the Dead Sea's shore?

Q788.t: A frozen ocean where the ice itself drifts
Q788.s: From a polar flight the Arctic Ocean looks like a cracked white plate: pack ice broken by dark lanes of open water called leads. It is the smallest and shallowest ocean, yet under the North Pole the sea is more than 4 km deep. In summer, pools of meltwater dot the ice with blue.
Q788.w: Endless white pack ice laced with dark cracks; in summer, turquoise meltwater ponds and patches of open sea.
f: There is no land at the North Pole — only drifting sea ice a few metres thick.
In 1893–1896 Nansen's ship Fram was deliberately frozen in and drifted with the ice across the Arctic.
Near the pole the sun stays up for about six months, then stays below the horizon for six.

q.q: What lies under the ice at the North Pole?

Q7354.t: The ocean that runs all the way around the world
Q7354.s: Few flights ever cross it, which makes this view rare. The Southern Ocean rings Antarctica with no land in its way, so its current circles the globe endlessly from west to east. Look for flat-topped icebergs — some are tens of kilometres long — and, in winter, a white apron of sea ice larger than the continent itself.
Q7354.w: Dark, wind-streaked water with scattered white icebergs; farther south, a solid rim of sea ice around Antarctica.
f: The Antarctic Circumpolar Current carries more water than any other current on Earth.
Sailors named its stormy latitudes the Roaring Forties, the Furious Fifties and the Screaming Sixties.
Its northern boundary is usually drawn at 60° South.

q.q: In which direction does the Antarctic Circumpolar Current flow?

Q98.t: Bigger than all the world's land put together
Q98.s: Hours of blue with barely a speck of land: this is the Pacific, covering about a third of the planet. Its deepest point, the Challenger Deep, lies nearly 11 km down — roughly as far below the surface as you are above it. Magellan called it the “peaceful sea” after the calm water he met in 1520.
Q98.w: Deep navy water to every horizon, broken only by rows of cloud and, now and then, the pale ring of an atoll.
f: The Pacific is larger than all the land on Earth combined.
Volcanoes and earthquake zones rim much of it — the so-called Ring of Fire.
Across the tropics it stretches nearly halfway around the globe.

q.q: Who named the Pacific after its calm, “peaceful” water?

Q1239.t: The warm ocean that powers the monsoon
Q1239.s: Sun glint on the Indian Ocean can blaze like hammered metal for minutes on end. This is the warmest of the oceans, and it is closed off in the north by Asia rather than open to the Arctic. That shape drives the monsoon: each summer the heating continent pulls in moist ocean air, bringing the rains to South Asia.
Q1239.w: Open blue ocean with a bright path of sun glint; in the tropics, rows of puffy cumulus over the water.
f: It covers about a fifth of the world's ocean area.
The Maldives, in its north, are some 1,200 small coral islands grouped into 26 atolls.
It is the only ocean named after a country — India.

q.q: How does the Indian Ocean rank in size among the oceans?

Q97.t: An ocean still growing, a few centimetres a year
Q97.s: Down the middle of the Atlantic, hidden under kilometres of water, runs the Mid-Atlantic Ridge — a volcanic seam where the sea floor is pulling apart. The ocean grows wider by a few centimetres every year, roughly as fast as your fingernails. At the surface, the sun's glint picks out the long, even lines of swell.
Q97.w: Open ocean ribbed with long swell, under drifting cloud fields; the sun's reflection shows the texture of the waves.
f: Iceland and the Azores are parts of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge that rise above the waves.
The North Atlantic is the busiest stretch of oceanic airspace in the world.
Its name comes from Atlas, the Titan of Greek myth who held up the sky.

q.q: Which island sits right on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge?

Q4918.t: The sea in the middle of the land
Q4918.s: Its famous deep blue comes from poverty, not richness: the water carries few nutrients and little plankton, so sunlight sinks deep. The Mediterranean joins the Atlantic only through the 14-km gap at Gibraltar. About six million years ago its link to the ocean closed and the sea almost dried out, leaving thick salt layers still buried under its floor.
Q4918.w: Intense cobalt-blue water between Europe and Africa, often with a sharp silver sun glint and scattered rocky islands.
f: Its name comes from the Latin for “in the middle of the land”.
Tides across most of it are small, usually well under half a metre.
More water evaporates than rivers bring in, so it is saltier than the open Atlantic.

q.q: About how wide is the Strait of Gibraltar at its narrowest?

Q5484.t: A “sea” that is really the world's largest lake
Q5484.s: Call it a sea, but it is the largest body of water on Earth with no outlet to the ocean — bigger than Germany. Its two ends are nothing alike: the shallow north, fed by the Volga, often freezes in winter, while the south plunges past 1,000 m. On the eastern shore look for Kara-Bogaz-Gol, a vivid turquoise lagoon.
Q5484.w: A huge inland sea with a pale, silty north and deep blue south; on its east side, the round turquoise Kara-Bogaz-Gol.
f: Its surface lies about 28 m below the level of the world ocean.
The Volga brings in roughly four-fifths of all the river water the Caspian receives.
For centuries it has been the world's main source of sturgeon and black caviar.

q.q: Which river supplies most of the Caspian Sea's water?

Q166.t: A turquoise surface over an oxygen-free deep
Q166.s: In late spring the Black Sea can turn milky turquoise, as blooms of chalk-plated plankton swirl across it. The depths are another world: below about 200 m there is no oxygen at all, and ancient wooden ships lie there almost untouched. It reaches the Mediterranean only through the narrow Bosphorus and Dardanelles.
Q166.w: A broad oval sea between Turkey, the Balkans and the Caucasus; in early summer, pale turquoise swirls on dark water.
f: Nearly 90% of its water holds no oxygen, only dissolved hydrogen sulphide.
In 2018 an intact Greek trading ship about 2,400 years old was found on its floor.
The Danube reaches it through a vast delta, one of Europe's largest wetlands.

q.q: What is missing from the Black Sea's deep water?

Q159183.t: A warm, deep nursery for typhoons
Q159183.s: This is some of the warmest open water on the planet, and it has a stormy talent: many of the Pacific's fiercest typhoons are born here. The sea is fenced by island chains — the Philippines, Taiwan, the Ryukyus and Japan to the west and north, the Marianas to the east. Far below the surface, trenches cut more than 10 km deep.
Q159183.w: Deep indigo ocean dotted with towering cumulus; island arcs mark its edges — Luzon and Taiwan to the west, the Marianas to the east.
f: The warm Kuroshio current sets off along its western edge and runs north past Japan.
The Philippine Trench, along its western side, drops to more than 10 km.
The sea sits on a tectonic plate of its own, the Philippine Sea Plate.

q.q: Which warm current runs north along the Philippine Sea's western edge?

Q82931.t: Home of the Great Barrier Reef
Q82931.s: The Coral Sea earns its name on its western side, where the Great Barrier Reef runs for about 2,300 km along Australia's coast. From above, the reefs look like turquoise brushstrokes and pale rings scattered on deep blue, with white surf on their seaward edges. Farther east the water deepens to a dark indigo.
Q82931.w: Turquoise reef patches and white surf lines off north-east Australia, fading into deep open blue to the east.
f: The Great Barrier Reef is made of nearly 3,000 separate reefs and hundreds of islands.
It is the largest structure built by living things, and it can be seen from orbit.
The reef has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1981.

q.q: About how long is the Great Barrier Reef?

Q33254.t: “The Ditch” between Australia and New Zealand
Q33254.s: Australians and New Zealanders call it “the Ditch”, but it is roughly 2,000 km across — about three hours in the air. The Tasman is known for rough water, stirred up by westerly winds from the Southern Ocean. Its name honours Abel Tasman, the Dutch navigator who crossed it in 1642 and sighted New Zealand.
Q33254.w: Open grey-blue water between two coastlines, often streaked with whitecaps and bands of cloud moving in from the west.
f: Lord Howe Island, in its western part, is a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Nearby Ball's Pyramid, a volcanic stack 562 m tall, rises straight out of the sea.
On its floor lies the Lord Howe Rise, part of Zealandia, a continent that is mostly underwater.

q.q: What do Australians and New Zealanders nickname the Tasman Sea?

Q38684.t: The world's largest bay, fed by the Ganges
Q38684.s: At the head of the bay, the Ganges and Brahmaputra pour out so much silt that the sea turns café-au-lait brown far from shore. This is the largest bay on Earth, and at its top lies the world's biggest delta, fringed by the tangled green of the Sundarbans mangroves. Farther south the silt settles and the water turns deep blue.
Q38684.w: A vast triangle of sea between India and Myanmar; near Bangladesh, brown silt plumes swirl into the blue.
f: The Sundarbans on its northern shore are the largest mangrove forest in the world.
Beneath the bay lies the Bengal Fan, a pile of river sediment some 3,000 km long.
River water makes its surface noticeably less salty than the open ocean.

q.q: Which rivers build the huge delta at the head of the Bay of Bengal?

Q37660.t: One of the busiest seaways on the planet
Q37660.s: In clear weather, look for faint white scratches on the blue — the wakes of ships. A huge share of the world's sea trade crosses this water between the Strait of Malacca, China, Japan and Korea. Scattered across the middle are low coral reefs and atolls, which show as turquoise rings where deep water suddenly gives way to shallows.
Q37660.w: Wide blue sea between Vietnam, the Philippines and southern China, with ship wakes and small turquoise reef rings.
f: Roughly a third of all global shipping passes through it.
The Mekong and the Pearl River both empty into it — the latter right beside Hong Kong.
Its deepest basin goes down more than 5,000 m.

q.q: Which great river's delta opens onto the South China Sea?

Q27092.t: Cloud streets by day, squid-boat lights by night
Q27092.s: On a winter flight, look for neat parallel lines of cloud streaming across the water from the Asian mainland: icy monsoon winds pick up moisture here and dump it as deep snow on Japan's western coast. At night the sea can sparkle with points of light — fishing boats using bright lamps to lure squid.
Q27092.w: An enclosed sea between Japan and the Asian mainland; in winter, rows of cloud stripes blowing towards Japan.
f: It connects to the open ocean only through a handful of narrow straits.
Its deepest basin reaches about 3,700 m.
In winter, sea ice forms in its far north, near the Tatar Strait.

q.q: What makes the Sea of Japan glitter at night?

Q58705.t: Monsoon sea between Arabia and India
Q58705.s: Every summer the south-west monsoon sweeps across the Arabian Sea, stirring cold, nutrient-rich water to the surface off Oman — plankton blooms can then paint the sea green. For thousands of years sailors rode these seasonal winds between Arabia and India in wooden dhows. In the north, the Indus fans out into a muddy delta.
Q58705.w: A wide sea between the Arabian Peninsula and India; in summer, greenish plankton swirls may show off Oman.
f: The Indus reaches the sea through a broad delta on Pakistan's coast.
Below the surface lies one of the largest oxygen-poor zones in any ocean.
A 1st-century Greek sailing guide, the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, describes trade across it.

q.q: Which great river flows into the Arabian Sea?

Q131274.t: Where the Mackenzie meets the Arctic ice
Q131274.s: For most of the year the Beaufort Sea is a white plain of drifting ice, turned slowly clockwise by a vast ocean eddy. In summer the ice pulls back from the coast, and the Mackenzie River spills a brown plume of silt from a delta braided with countless lakes. Look for that tea-coloured stain against the ice.
Q131274.w: Sea ice north of Alaska and Canada; in summer, a brown river plume and a lake-speckled delta on the Canadian shore.
f: It is named after Admiral Francis Beaufort, who devised the wind-force scale.
The Mackenzie, Canada's longest river, builds a huge delta on its shore.
Bowhead whales pass through it every year on their seasonal migration.

q.q: The Beaufort Sea's namesake is known for devising what?

Q1247.t: Turquoise shallows beside deep blue water
Q1247.s: The famous colours are real: over sandbanks and reefs the Caribbean glows turquoise and jade, with white sand showing through. Just off those shallows the floor drops away to deep blue — in the Cayman Trough it lies about 7,700 m down. The sea is fenced in by the arc of the Antilles, a chain of islands curving from Cuba almost to Venezuela.
Q1247.w: Turquoise and emerald shallows around islands, white sand bars, and a sharp edge where the water turns deep blue.
f: It takes its name from the Caribs, a people of the Lesser Antilles.
The Mesoamerican Barrier Reef off Belize and Mexico is the largest reef system in the Americas.
The Panama Canal links it to the Pacific across a narrow isthmus.

q.q: Which people is the Caribbean Sea named after?

Q12630.t: A warm basin with a bird's-foot delta
Q12630.s: Where the Mississippi reaches the Gulf, its delta splays out like a bird's foot, trailing brown silt into the blue. The Gulf is a warm, nearly round basin, and at night hundreds of offshore oil and gas platforms scatter lights across it. Buried off Yucatán lies the crater of the asteroid that ended the age of the dinosaurs.
Q12630.w: A broad, rounded gulf; off Louisiana, the Mississippi's fingered delta and brown plume; at night, scattered platform lights offshore.
f: The Chicxulub crater, about 180 km across, lies partly beneath its floor.
Padre Island, off the Texas coast, is the longest barrier island in the world.
The warm Loop Current flows in between Yucatán and Cuba and leaves past Florida.

q.q: What shape is the Mississippi Delta famous for?

Q184189.t: Iceberg highway between Greenland and Labrador
Q184189.s: Many flights between Europe and North America cross this cold sea between Greenland and Labrador. In spring and early summer, look for white specks on dark water: icebergs calved from Greenland's glaciers, riding the Labrador Current south towards Newfoundland. In winter, surface water here grows so cold and dense that it sinks deep, helping drive the ocean's slow global circulation.
Q184189.w: Dark open water between Greenland's southern tip and the Labrador coast; in spring, scattered white icebergs and drifting pack ice.
f: Norse sagas describe Markland, a forested coast thought to be Labrador, reached around AD 1000.
The cold Labrador Current flows south along its western side, carrying icebergs and sea ice.
Cape Farewell, the southern tip of Greenland, marks its north-eastern corner.

q.q: Where do most icebergs in the Labrador Sea come from?

Q3040.t: An inland sea that freezes over every winter
Q3040.s: Hudson Bay is a true sea set inside a continent, and each winter it freezes over almost completely. Look at its eastern coast: it bends in a smooth, near-perfect arc, as if traced around a giant plate. The land around the bay is still slowly rising, springing back now that the weight of the ice-age glaciers is gone.
Q3040.w: A vast, roughly round bay in northern Canada — white ice in winter, dark water in late summer; note the smooth eastern arc.
f: The smooth curve of its eastern shore is known as the Nastapoka Arc.
The land around it is still rising by about a centimetre a year since the last ice age.
Each autumn polar bears gather near Churchill, waiting for the bay to freeze so they can hunt seals.

q.q: What are Churchill's polar bears waiting for each autumn?

Q37040.t: Iceberg-strewn water between Baffin Island and Greenland
Q37040.s: On a clear day Baffin Bay is all contrast: Greenland's white ice cap and glacier tongues on one side, the snowy mountains of Baffin Island on the other. Icebergs from glaciers such as Ilulissat drift across the water like scattered sugar cubes. In winter most of the bay freezes — except the North Water in the far north, which stays open.
Q37040.w: A long bay between Greenland's ice-covered coast and Baffin Island; white icebergs dot the dark water in summer.
f: The North Water is one of the largest patches of Arctic sea that stays open through the winter.
Ilulissat Icefjord on its Greenland shore, a UNESCO site, sends huge icebergs into the bay.
It is named after William Baffin, who sailed and charted it in 1616.

q.q: What is the North Water in Baffin Bay?
q.a: Sea that stays ice-free in winter
x: A freshwater lake on an island

Q180531.t: Where glaciers pour down to the sea
Q180531.s: Few coasts look wilder from the air. Along the Gulf of Alaska, ice fields spill glaciers straight towards the sea, and the Malaspina Glacier spreads across the coastal plain in a huge lobe striped like marble cake. Where silty meltwater meets clear ocean, you may see a sharp line between milky green and deep blue.
Q180531.w: The curving southern coast of Alaska: snowy peaks, glacier tongues, and the vast rounded lobe of the Malaspina Glacier.
f: The Malaspina is one of the world's largest piedmont glaciers — ice that spreads out over flat land.
Mount Saint Elias, 5,489 m high, rises close to the gulf's northern shore.
Kodiak Island, on its western side, is home to the huge Kodiak brown bear.

q.q: About how high is Mount Saint Elias, above the Gulf of Alaska?

Q23406.t: A young ocean being born between Africa and Arabia
Q23406.s: The Red Sea is an ocean in the making: Africa and Arabia are slowly pulling apart, and the crack between them has flooded. From the air it's a long, narrow blue channel between desert coasts, fringed with turquoise reefs. In the north it splits around the Sinai into two horns — the Gulfs of Suez and Aqaba.
Q23406.w: A long, slender sea between brown desert shores, with turquoise coral fringes; at its top, two arms around the Sinai triangle.
f: No permanent river flows into it, and it is one of the saltiest seas connected to the ocean.
Africa and Arabia are drifting apart here by roughly a centimetre a year.
Since 1869 the Suez Canal has linked its northern tip to the Mediterranean.

q.q: Which two gulfs form the Red Sea's northern “horns”?

Q41602.t: A northern sea whose ice reaches Hokkaido
Q41602.s: In winter the Sea of Okhotsk turns white far to the south: its drift ice reaches the coast of Hokkaido, at roughly the latitude of Venice. The sea is walled in by Kamchatka to the east, Sakhalin to the west and the long chain of Kuril volcanoes to the south-east. In summer, fog often hides the water.
Q41602.w: A broad northern sea between Kamchatka, Sakhalin and the Kuril arc; white with ice in winter, often under fog in summer.
f: Winter drift ice here reaches Hokkaido's coast at around 44° North.
The Kuril Islands, a chain of volcanoes, separate it from the open Pacific.
Okhotsk, founded on its shore in the 1640s, was the first Russian settlement on the Pacific.

q.q: Which island's coast does Okhotsk drift ice reach in the south?

Q173343.t: Home of the clearest seawater ever measured
Q173343.s: The Weddell Sea is ruled by ice. Its pack ice turns in a slow clockwise gyre that trapped Shackleton's ship Endurance in 1915 and crushed it; the crew all survived, and the wreck was found in 2022 some 3 km down. To the south lies the Filchner–Ronne Ice Shelf, a floating plain of ice ending in cliffs tens of metres high.
Q173343.w: A vast sheet of pack ice east of the Antarctic Peninsula, ending at the flat white cliff of a floating ice shelf.
f: In 1986 a white disc lowered into its water stayed visible to 79 m — the clearest seawater ever recorded.
The Filchner–Ronne Ice Shelf at its southern end is one of the largest floating ice shelves on Earth.
It is named after James Weddell, a British sealer who sailed deep into it in 1823.

q.q: Whose ship was crushed by the Weddell Sea's ice in 1915?

Q34675.t: Shallow, warm, and dotted with man-made islands
Q34675.s: This is a shallow, bath-warm sea — on average only about 50 m deep, with summer surface water often above 30 °C. Look off Dubai for the unmistakable fronds of the palm-shaped artificial islands, and for Qatar jutting north like a thumb. At night, gas flares and city lights ring the water. Before oil, its wealth came from pearls.
Q34675.w: A shallow turquoise gulf between Iran and Arabia; spot Qatar's thumb-shaped peninsula and Dubai's palm-shaped islands.
f: The Tigris and Euphrates reach it together through the Shatt al-Arab.
Its only outlet to the ocean is the Strait of Hormuz, less than 40 km wide at its narrowest.
For centuries pearl diving was the main livelihood of towns on its Arabian shore.

q.q: Which peninsula juts into the Persian Gulf like a thumb?

Q164466.t: The sea at the foot of the great ice barrier
Q164466.s: The Ross Sea ends in a wall. Its southern edge is the Ross Ice Shelf, a floating slab of ice roughly the size of France, whose cliffs early explorers simply called “the Barrier”. On Ross Island, Mount Erebus sends up steam from a lava lake in its crater. Nowhere does open sea reach closer to the South Pole.
Q164466.w: Dark water and pack ice ending at a flat, sharp-edged white plateau of floating ice; to the west, snowy volcanic Ross Island.
f: The ice shelf's front rises tens of metres above the sea and runs for some 600 km.
Mount Erebus, 3,794 m high, is the southernmost active volcano on Earth.
Much of the Ross Sea has been a marine protected area since 2017.

q.q: The Ross Ice Shelf is roughly the size of which country?

Q5525.t: The biggest lake wholly in Canada, on the Arctic Circle
Q5525.s: Great Bear Lake sprawls across the northern forest and tundra in five long arms, like a starfish pressed into the land. The Arctic Circle crosses its northern part, and ice often lingers on the water into July. It is the largest lake lying entirely inside Canada, and it is almost untouched: only one community, Déline, sits on its shore.
Q5525.w: A huge, many-armed lake in the far north-west of Canada, white or streaked with ice for much of the year.
f: Its outflow, the Great Bear River, runs into the Mackenzie.
A 33-kg lake trout caught here in 1995 set a rod-and-reel world record.
The lake and its watershed form Tsá Tué, a UNESCO biosphere reserve.

q.q: Which line crosses Great Bear Lake?

Q5539.s: Great Slave Lake has two faces. The main western basin is broad and open, while the East Arm is a maze of cliffs, islands and deep channels — the lake reaches 614 m there, deeper than any other in North America. The territorial capital, Yellowknife, sits on the north shore, and the Mackenzie River slips out of the western end.
Q5539.w: A wide lake with a long, island-studded eastern arm; at night, Yellowknife's lights on the north shore.
f: Its name comes from the Slavey, a Dene people, not from slavery.
In winter an ice road across the frozen lake links Yellowknife with the community of Dettah.
Ice covers the lake for roughly half of every year.

q.q: How deep is Great Slave Lake at its deepest?

Q3272.t: A shallow giant left behind by an ice-age lake
Q3272.s: Lake Winnipeg stretches north for over 400 km, pinched at the waist where its northern and southern basins meet at the Narrows. For all its size it is shallow — about 12 m on average — and in summer, algae blooms can swirl across it in shades of green visible from the air. Its name means “muddy water” in Cree.
Q3272.w: A long lake north of the city of Winnipeg, pinched in the middle; often greenish in late summer.
f: It is a remnant of glacial Lake Agassiz, which once covered more area than all of today's Great Lakes.
Its outflow, the Nelson River, carries its water north to Hudson Bay.
Its drainage basin reaches all the way to the Rocky Mountains.

q.q: What does the Cree name “Winnipeg” mean?

Q5492.t: The shallow, warm Great Lake that feeds Niagara
Q5492.s: Lake Erie is the shallowest of the Great Lakes, so it warms fastest in summer and is the one most likely to freeze over in winter. From above, look for Long Point, a slender sand spit curving about 40 km out from the Canadian shore. The lake's water leaves eastward, over Niagara Falls.
Q5492.w: A long oval lake between Ontario and Ohio; look for the thin hooked spit of Long Point on the northern shore.
f: It averages only about 19 m deep — far less than the other Great Lakes.
Point Pelee, jutting into its western part, is the southern tip of mainland Canada.
In late summer, green algae blooms in its western basin can be seen from space.

q.q: Which of the Great Lakes is the shallowest?

Q1062.t: The last Great Lake before the sea
Q1062.s: This is the final step in the Great Lakes' staircase: water arrives down the Niagara River and leaves through the St Lawrence towards the Atlantic. Lake Ontario is the smallest of the five by area, yet deep enough that it rarely freezes over. At night, look for the dense glow of Toronto and its suburbs wrapped around the western shore.
Q1062.w: An oval lake with Toronto's urban sprawl on its north-west shore; at its eastern end, a scatter of islands.
f: The St Lawrence leaves it among the Thousand Islands — in fact there are more than 1,800.
Its deepest point is about 244 m.
Winds crossing it dump heavy lake-effect snow on New York's Tug Hill Plateau.

q.q: Which river carries Lake Ontario's water to the Atlantic?

Q1066.t: The largest freshwater lake on Earth by area
Q1066.s: Lake Superior is big enough to have its own horizon: at 563 km long, even from cruise height you may not see it end to end. No freshwater lake on Earth covers more area, and its cold, clear water holds about a tenth of all the fresh water on the planet's surface. In winter, ice and snow trace its rocky outline in white.
Q1066.w: A vast lake shaped a little like a wolf's head facing west, with the long Keweenaw Peninsula jutting from its southern shore.
f: A drop of water that enters it stays, on average, for almost 200 years.
Isle Royale, in its north-west, has hosted a study of wolves and moose since 1958 — one of the longest of its kind.
Its deepest point lies 406 m below the surface.

q.q: On average, how long does water stay in Lake Superior?

Q1169.t: The only Great Lake wholly in the United States
Q1169.s: Lake Michigan hangs down from the Straits of Mackinac like a long blue pendant, with Chicago's grid pressed against its south-western corner. Its eastern shore is lined with pale sand dunes, some rising over 100 m above the water. Strictly speaking, it is one lake with Huron: the two meet at the Straits and share the same level.
Q1169.w: A long north–south lake: Chicago's sprawl at the south-west, pale dune shores along the east, the Mackinac straits at the top.
f: Its eastern shore holds the largest freshwater sand dunes in the world.
The Mackinac Bridge, about 8 km long, spans the straits that link it to Lake Huron.
Its name comes from an Ojibwe word meaning “great water”.

q.q: Which lake is Lake Michigan hydrologically joined with?

Q1383.t: The Great Lake with tens of thousands of islands
Q1383.s: Lake Huron is the island lake of the five. Along its north and east, the granite shore breaks into thousands of rocky islets, and Manitoulin — the largest island in any freshwater lake on Earth — divides the main lake from the North Channel. Georgian Bay, almost a lake in its own right, opens to the east.
Q1383.w: A broad lake east of Michigan's mitten; the long island of Manitoulin in the north and Georgian Bay to the east.
f: Counting all its islands, it has the longest shoreline of the Great Lakes.
Saginaw Bay cuts into Michigan's shore, separating the “thumb” from the rest of the mitten.
The French named it after the Huron, or Wendat, people.

q.q: Which Lake Huron island is the largest in any freshwater lake?

Q5532.t: A lake with more fish species than any other
Q5532.s: Lake Malawi fills a long trench of the East African Rift, a slim blue blade about 580 km long hemmed in by steep escarpments. Beneath the surface swim more fish species than in any other lake on Earth — hundreds of brightly coloured cichlids, most of them found nowhere else. At night, fishermen's lamps can speckle the dark water.
Q5532.w: A long, narrow lake running north–south in the Rift Valley, with mountains rising steeply along its northern shores.
f: Its deepest point is more than 700 m down.
Lake Malawi National Park, at its southern end, is a UNESCO World Heritage site.
It is also called Lake Nyasa, and Lago Niassa in Mozambique.

q.q: Which fish make up most of Lake Malawi's famous variety?

Q5511.t: The longest freshwater lake in the world
Q5511.s: Lake Tanganyika runs for about 670 km along the floor of the Rift Valley, farther than any other freshwater lake. It is narrow — about 50 km wide on average — but plunges to 1,470 m, second only to Baikal. Its long, steep shores are shared by four countries, and the water is a deep, clear blue.
Q5511.w: A very long, narrow lake running north–south in a deep rift, lined by steep mountain walls on both sides.
f: Tanzania, DR Congo, Burundi and Zambia share its shores.
In 1871 Stanley found Livingstone at Ujiji, on its eastern shore.
It is among the oldest lakes on Earth, formed roughly 10 million years ago.

q.q: Which lake is deeper than Lake Tanganyika?

Q5505.t: Africa's largest lake, where the White Nile begins
Q5505.s: Lake Victoria is so wide it looks like an inland sea, with a ragged coastline of bays, peninsulas and green islands. It is Africa's largest lake, yet surprisingly shallow — only about 80 m at its deepest. The equator crosses its northern waters, and from its northern shore the White Nile slips out on its long journey to the Mediterranean.
Q5505.w: A huge lake straddling the equator, with a jagged shoreline, many islands and afternoon thunderclouds building over the water.
f: It is the largest tropical lake in the world and the second-largest freshwater lake by area.
John Hanning Speke named it after Queen Victoria in 1858; “Nyanza” simply means “lake” in several local languages.
Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania share its waters.

q.q: Which great river flows out of Lake Victoria?

Q173862.t: A freshwater sea with a two-volcano island
Q173862.s: Look for Ometepe: an island shaped like a figure of eight, formed by two volcanic cones joined by a low neck of land. It rises from the largest lake in Central America, so wide that the Spanish called it the Mar Dulce, the sweet sea. Bull sharks have long swum here from the Caribbean, up the San Juan River.
Q173862.w: A broad lake in south-west Nicaragua; spot the twin volcanic cones of Ometepe island near its western shore.
f: Ometepe's taller volcano, Concepción, is active and rises to about 1,600 m.
Near the city of Granada, hundreds of tiny islets, Las Isletas, are scattered along the shore.
The lake drains to the Caribbean through the San Juan River.

q.q: What forms the island of Ometepe?

Q1134446.t: A clear, island-studded lake of the Canadian Shield
Q1134446.s: Reindeer Lake is pure Canadian Shield: a long sheet of dark, clear water scattered with rocky, forested islands, its shores carved into countless bays by ice-age glaciers. It stretches north–south through almost roadless forest. Its water drains south through the Reindeer River into the Churchill, and on to Hudson Bay.
Q1134446.w: A long north–south lake with ragged shores and many rocky islands, set in dark forest in north-eastern Saskatchewan.
f: It is the second-largest lake in Saskatchewan, after Lake Athabasca.
The Cree community of Southend sits at its southern tip.
Its cold, clear water is home to big lake trout and northern pike.

q.q: Where does Reindeer Lake's water finally end up?

Q845876.t: A maze of islands with a notch in the border
Q845876.s: From above, Lake of the Woods looks like two lakes in one: an open, rounded basin in the south, and in the north a shattered maze of some 14,500 rocky, forested islands. On its western side sits the Northwest Angle, a quirk of old map-making that leaves a piece of Minnesota north of the 49th parallel, reachable by land only through Canada.
Q845876.w: A lake on the Canada–US border: an open southern bay and a northern labyrinth of wooded islands.
f: The Northwest Angle is the only part of the contiguous United States north of the 49th parallel.
Its water drains north through the Winnipeg River.
The town of Kenora, Ontario, sits at its northern outlet.

q.q: About how many islands does Lake of the Woods have?

Q122184.t: The big lake that feeds Lake Superior
Q122184.s: Just north of Lake Superior lies a big, ragged lake scattered with hundreds of islands. Lake Nipigon is the largest lake entirely inside Ontario, and it drains south through the Nipigon River — the biggest river flowing into Superior. Around it stretches almost unbroken boreal forest, dark green in summer and white in winter.
Q122184.w: A large, island-dotted lake a short way north of Lake Superior's northern shore, surrounded by dark forest.
f: The world-record brook trout, 6.6 kg, was caught in the Nipigon River in 1915.
The lake covers about 4,800 km².

q.q: Into which Great Lake does Lake Nipigon drain?

Q645901.t: The lake that gave a province its name
Q645901.s: Lake Manitoba is long and shallow, and halfway along it narrows to a slim neck called the Narrows. There, waves striking limestone shores make eerie booming sounds, which people heard as the drum of a spirit — the likely origin of the lake's name, and of the province named after it. It is nowhere much deeper than 7 m.
Q645901.w: A long, slender lake west of Lake Winnipeg, narrowing sharply halfway up; marshes fringe its southern end.
f: Delta Marsh, on its southern shore, is one of the largest freshwater marshes in North America.
Its water flows on, through smaller rivers and lakes, into Lake Winnipeg.

q.q: What was named after Lake Manitoba?

Q934638.s: Three big lakes lie side by side in Manitoba, all remnants of the same vanished ice-age lake. Winnipegosis is the westernmost: long, narrow and shallow, with a shoreline of low points and quiet bays. Even its name is the little sister of Winnipeg's — roughly “little muddy water” in Cree. Its water flows south into Lake Manitoba.
Q934638.w: The westernmost of Manitoba's three great lakes: long and narrow, running north–south, west of Lake Winnipeg.
f: It drains south into Lake Manitoba through the Waterhen River.
Lakes Winnipegosis, Manitoba and Winnipeg are all remnants of glacial Lake Agassiz.
It covers more than 5,000 km², yet over most of that area it is only a few metres deep.

q.q: Which lake does Lake Winnipegosis flow into directly?

Q272463.t: A northern lake with a desert on its shore
Q272463.s: Along the south shore of Lake Athabasca, the dark forest suddenly gives way to bare, pale sand: the Athabasca Sand Dunes, among the most northerly large active dunes on Earth. At the lake's western end, the Peace and Athabasca rivers build a vast green delta. The north shore is rocky Canadian Shield, pitted with small lakes.
Q272463.w: A long east–west lake on the Alberta–Saskatchewan border; look for pale patches of sand along its southern shore.
f: The Peace–Athabasca Delta is one of the largest freshwater deltas in the world.
Fort Chipewyan, founded on its shore in 1788, is one of Alberta's oldest settlements.
Its water flows north via the Slave River towards Great Slave Lake and the Arctic.

q.q: What unusual landscape lies on Lake Athabasca's southern shore?

Q1458051.t: Quebec's largest natural lake, split by islands
Q1458051.s: Lake Mistassini looks as if it was raked by a giant comb: long and narrow, it runs north-east for more than 150 km, with a chain of slender islands dividing it lengthwise. The Cree community of Mistissini sits on its southern shore, and the lake drains west through the Rupert River into James Bay.
Q1458051.w: A long, narrow lake running south-west to north-east in the forests of central Quebec, split down the middle by islands.
f: Its name comes from the Cree for “big rock”.
It covers about 2,300 km², more than any other natural lake in Quebec.

q.q: Where does Lake Mistassini's water end up?

Q1267413.t: Lake Huron's big bay of thirty thousand islands
Q1267413.s: Georgian Bay is so large it is sometimes called the sixth Great Lake, though it is really an arm of Lake Huron. The Bruce Peninsula walls it off in the west, a finger of limestone cliffs above turquoise water. Along the eastern shore, pinkish granite breaks into the Thirty Thousand Islands, a glittering scatter from the air.
Q1267413.w: A large bay east of Lake Huron, closed off by the finger of the Bruce Peninsula, with a maze of islands on its eastern shore.
f: The Thirty Thousand Islands form the world's largest freshwater archipelago.
The Bruce Peninsula is part of the Niagara Escarpment, the same rock ridge that Niagara Falls pours over.
It was named in 1822 after King George IV.

q.q: Which peninsula separates Georgian Bay from the rest of Lake Huron?

Q15288.t: Europe's largest lake, rocky in the north
Q15288.s: Europe's largest lake has two faces. Its southern shore is low and marshy, but the north breaks into skerries — rocky islands and narrow inlets gouged by glaciers — where the water plunges to over 200 m. On the Valaam islands, in the north, stands a monastery founded in the Middle Ages.
Q15288.w: A huge lake north-east of St Petersburg, low-shored in the south; in the north, a rocky maze of islands and inlets.
f: The Neva carries its water only about 74 km to the Baltic, straight through St Petersburg.
It is home to the Ladoga ringed seal, a subspecies found nowhere else.
The lake covers about 17,700 km² — more than half the size of Belgium.

q.q: Which river carries Lake Ladoga's water to the Baltic?

Q134485.t: A lake that is half fresh and half salty
Q134485.s: Lake Balkhash is a long, thin arc across the Kazakh steppe, some 600 km from end to end, and it is two lakes in one. The western half, fed by the Ili River, is nearly fresh; the eastern half, linked to it only by a narrow strait, is salty. From above, the two halves often show slightly different shades.
Q134485.w: A long, thin arc of water across the dry steppe of eastern Kazakhstan, with the green Ili delta near its western end.
f: The Ili River, flowing in from the south, supplies most of its water.
The strait linking its two halves is only a few kilometres wide.
It has no outlet: water leaves only by evaporation.

q.q: Which river feeds Lake Balkhash?

Q125888.t: A rift-valley lake the Nile passes through
Q125888.s: Lake Albert lies in a deep trough of the western Rift Valley, walled by steep escarpments — on the Congo side they rise abruptly for hundreds of metres. The Nile only brushes its northern tip: the Victoria Nile flows in below Murchison Falls, and the Albert Nile leaves a few kilometres away. The lake stretches about 160 km from south-west to north-east.
Q125888.w: A long, narrow lake between steep escarpments on the Uganda–Congo border, with green papyrus flats at its northern end.
f: Samuel Baker reached it in 1864 and named it after Prince Albert, Queen Victoria's late husband.
The Semliki River flows in at its southern end, carrying water from the Rwenzori Mountains.

q.q: Who named Lake Albert in 1864?

Q173596.t: Sweden's inland sea, split into two basins
Q173596.s: Sweden's biggest lake has two parts: the broad main basin and, to the south-west, the smaller Dalbosjön, almost cut off by two peninsulas reaching towards each other. Rocky islands and skerries dot the water, and at Karlstad on the northern shore the Klarälven river fans out into a delta. Vänern is the largest lake in the European Union.
Q173596.w: A huge lake in south-west Sweden, pinched into two basins by peninsulas, with rocky islands and a delta at Karlstad in the north.
f: Its water leaves through the Göta älv, reaching the sea at Gothenburg.
The Göta Canal links it eastwards to Lake Vättern and on to the Baltic.
It covers about 5,600 km².

q.q: Which city stands at the mouth of the river draining Vänern?

Q166162.t: Europe's second-largest lake, with fingers in the north
Q166162.s: Look at Lake Onega's northern end: it splits into long, narrow bays lying side by side like the fingers of a hand, shaped by the ice sheets. The south is a broad, open basin. Among the northern islands lies Kizhi, whose wooden Church of the Transfiguration is crowned with 22 domes — far too small to spot from here, but worth knowing about.
Q166162.w: A big lake north-east of Ladoga, its northern end split into long parallel bays; Petrozavodsk on the western shore.
f: The wooden churches of Kizhi are a UNESCO World Heritage site.
More than a thousand rock carvings, thousands of years old, cover granite ledges on its eastern shore.
The Svir River carries its water west into Lake Ladoga.

q.q: How many domes crown the Church of the Transfiguration on Kizhi?

Q116685.t: The lake where the Blue Nile begins
Q116685.s: High on the Ethiopian plateau, about 1,800 m up, Lake Tana is the source of the Blue Nile, which slips out of its southern shore at Bahir Dar. Its islands and peninsulas shelter old monasteries with painted churches, and fishermen still paddle papyrus boats called tankwa. From the air it's a broad, rounded lake ringed by green farmland.
Q116685.w: A broad, roundish lake on the green Ethiopian highlands, with Bahir Dar and the Blue Nile's outflow at its southern tip.
f: The Blue Nile supplies most of the water that flows down the Nile through Egypt.
About 30 km downstream, the Blue Nile plunges over the Tis Issat falls.
Some of its island monasteries date back to the 14th century.

q.q: Which river flows out of Lake Tana?

Q35342.t: A deep-blue lake at 3,800 m, with floating islands
Q35342.s: Lake Titicaca sits at about 3,810 m — more than a third of the way up to your cruising height — and its water looks an intense, dark blue in the thin mountain air. Beyond it rise the snowy peaks of Bolivia's Cordillera Real. On its Peruvian side, the Uros people live on floating islands built from totora reeds.
Q35342.w: A large, irregular deep-blue lake on the bare high plateau, with snow-capped mountains rising along its eastern side.
f: It is often called the highest navigable lake in the world.
Its two basins are joined by the narrow Strait of Tiquina.
In Inca legend, the founders of the Inca dynasty rose from its waters.

q.q: What are the Uros people's floating islands made of?

Q192770.t: A labyrinth of water and 14,000 islands
Q192770.s: From above, Saimaa hardly looks like a lake at all — more like a jigsaw of blue channels, pine-dark islands and narrow sounds spread across eastern Finland. It has around 14,000 islands and a shoreline so convoluted that it runs to about 15,000 km. In winter the whole maze freezes into a white puzzle.
Q192770.w: A sprawling maze of lakes, channels and forested islands across south-eastern Finland, with no single open expanse.
f: The Saimaa ringed seal lives here and nowhere else; only a few hundred remain.
The Saimaa Canal links it to the Gulf of Finland at Vyborg.
It is the largest lake in Finland.

q.q: Which rare animal lives only in Lake Saimaa?

Q375029.t: A man-made “sea” over a drowned town
Q375029.s: Locals call it the Rybinsk Sea, and from the air it earns the name: a broad sheet of grey-blue water spreading north from the Volga over flat forest and fields. Created in the 1940s by damming the Volga and Sheksna, it was then the largest man-made lake in the world. Beneath it lies the old town of Mologa.
Q375029.w: A wide, shallow, many-armed reservoir north of Rybinsk, filling the flooded valleys of the Volga, Sheksna and Mologa.
f: Its average depth is only about 5–6 m.
Rafts of floating peat, sometimes carrying bushes and small trees, drift across it.
The Darwin Nature Reserve on its shore was set up to study how the flooding changed nature.

q.q: Which town was flooded to create the Rybinsk Reservoir?

Q21890573.t: Australia's lowest point, a salt pan that rarely fills
Q21890573.s: Most of the time Kati Thanda–Lake Eyre is a vast, glaring-white salt pan about 15 m below sea level — the lowest point in Australia. Only after big rains far to the north does water spread across it, sometimes tinted pink by salt-loving algae. Then pelicans fly in from the coast, hundreds of kilometres away, to breed.
Q21890573.w: A huge white salt pan in the South Australian outback, sometimes streaked with shallow blue or pink water.
f: Its catchment covers about a sixth of Australia.
In 1964 Donald Campbell set a land speed record of about 649 km/h on its salt.
It has filled completely only a few times since Europeans first saw it.

q.q: How far below sea level is the bed of Kati Thanda–Lake Eyre?

Q178741.t: A lake cut in two: pink on one side, blue on the other
Q178741.s: Look for a dead-straight line across the water: a railway causeway completed in 1959 splits Great Salt Lake in two. North of it the brine is so salty that microbes turn it pink or rusty red; south of it the water stays blue-green. The lake is what remains of Lake Bonneville, an ice-age lake that once covered much of western Utah.
Q178741.w: A large, shallow lake west of Salt Lake City, crossed by a straight causeway: pinkish-red water north, blue-green south.
f: It is the largest saltwater lake in the Western Hemisphere.
Antelope Island, its largest island, is home to a free-roaming bison herd.
Tiny brine shrimp thrive in it, and their eggs are harvested as fish-farm feed.

q.q: What turns the north arm of Great Salt Lake pink?

Q276776.t: A vanishing sea, turned into a new desert
Q276776.s: What you see is the ghost of a sea. In 1960 the Aral was the world's fourth-largest lake, but its rivers were diverted to irrigate cotton, and it shrank. The southern part split into remnants: a deep western basin and a pale, shifting eastern one that dried out almost entirely in 2014. Its old seabed is now a new desert, the Aralkum.
Q276776.w: A narrow strip of dark water in the west and pale salt flats to the east, ringed by old shorelines in the desert.
f: The old fishing port of Moynaq now lies more than 100 km from the water, with rusting ships in the sand.
The former Vozrozhdeniya Island is now joined to the mainland.
Salt and dust blown off the dry seabed can travel hundreds of kilometres.

q.q: Why did the Aral Sea shrink?
q.a: Its rivers were diverted for irrigation
x: A canal emptied it into the Caspian

Q876280.t: The “little” lagoon that is 180 km long
Q876280.s: Its name means “little” in Tupi-Guarani, yet Lagoa Mirim stretches about 180 km along the coastal plain, shared by Brazil and Uruguay. Only a strip of sand dunes and marshes separates it from the Atlantic. From the air, look for its brownish, silty water beside the ocean's blue, with green rice paddies spread along its western shore.
Q876280.w: A long lagoon parallel to the Atlantic coast near the Brazil–Uruguay border, separated from the sea by a sandy strip.
f: The São Gonçalo Channel links it to the even larger Lagoa dos Patos to the north-east.
The Taim wetlands, a reserve rich in waterbirds, lie between the lagoon and the sea.

q.q: What does “Mirim” mean in Tupi-Guarani?

Q42191.t: The “warm lake” of the Tian Shan that never freezes
Q42191.s: Issyk-Kul is a long sapphire oval held between two snowy ranges of the Tian Shan, about 1,600 m above sea level. Winters in these mountains are harsh, yet the lake never freezes — its name means “warm lake” in Kyrgyz. It is deep, slightly salty and strikingly clear, and for most of the year its blue is framed by white peaks.
Q42191.w: A long east–west oval of deep blue between two parallel snow-capped ranges in north-eastern Kyrgyzstan.
f: It reaches about 668 m deep.
No river flows out of it, which is why its water is slightly salty.
It is one of the largest mountain lakes in the world.

q.q: What does the name Issyk-Kul mean?

Q3358037.t: The part of the Aral that is coming back
Q3358037.s: Unlike its southern neighbour, the North Aral Sea is a rare story of recovery. In 2005 the Kokaral Dam sealed it off from the shrinking south, so the Syr Darya's water now stays here. The level rose, the water grew less salty, and fish returned. From above it's a lobed blue lake set in pale desert, still well short of its old shores.
Q3358037.w: A lobed blue lake in the desert of south-western Kazakhstan; a dam at its southern tip, the Syr Darya entering from the east.
f: The Kokaral Dam, about 13 km long, holds its water back.
The water has crept back towards Aralsk, a port that had been left far inland.
Commercial fishing has returned to its waters.

q.q: What helped the North Aral Sea to recover?

Q19270.t: A deep tropical basin in the Coral Triangle
Q19270.s: Ringed by Mindanao, Sulawesi and Borneo, this almost enclosed basin drops to more than 6,000 m. Its open water is a dark, velvety blue, but the edges shine turquoise wherever reefs fringe the islands. The Celebes Sea is part of the Coral Triangle, where more kinds of coral and reef fish live than anywhere else on Earth.
Q19270.w: A deep-blue sea between Mindanao, Sulawesi's long northern arm and north-east Borneo; volcanic islands along its eastern edge.
f: “Celebes” is the old European name for the island of Sulawesi.
The Sulu Archipelago, a chain of small islands, separates it from the Sulu Sea.

q.q: “Celebes” is the old name of which island?

Q160194.t: Coral atolls in the heart of the Philippine seas
Q160194.s: The Sulu Sea is ringed by islands. Look for the long, thin island of Palawan — it forms the north-western wall, like a green spine laid on the blue. In the middle of the open water, far from any coast, lie the Tubbataha Reefs: two atolls whose turquoise lagoons and white sand cays stand out sharply against the deep blue.
Q160194.w: A deep-blue sea between Palawan, Mindanao and the central Philippine islands, with small turquoise atolls in the middle.
f: The Tubbataha Reefs have been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1993.
Its deep basin plunges to more than 5,000 m.
The Sulu Archipelago, which gives the sea its name, runs along its south-eastern edge.

q.q: Which long island forms the Sulu Sea's north-western edge?

Q47545.t: An Arctic sea kept open by warm Atlantic water
Q47545.s: Although much of it lies north of the Arctic Circle, the Norwegian Sea stays almost free of ice all year: a branch of the Gulf Stream's warm water flows through it towards the Arctic. On the Norwegian side, look for the jagged peaks of the Lofoten Islands rising straight from the water like a row of shark's teeth.
Q47545.w: Open grey-blue sea off Norway's coast; to the east, the saw-toothed Lofoten chain and a coastline shredded into fjords.
f: Off the tip of Lofoten swirls the Moskstraumen, the maelstrom that inspired Edgar Allan Poe and Jules Verne.
The Røst Reef off Lofoten is the largest cold-water coral reef yet discovered.
Its deep basins go down more than 3,000 m.

q.q: Which famous whirlpool swirls off the Lofoten Islands?

Q132868.t: The Arctic's exit door for drifting sea ice
Q132868.s: Most of the sea ice that leaves the Arctic Ocean does so through here. Floes squeeze out through Fram Strait, between Greenland and Svalbard, then ride the East Greenland Current south along the coast in a long white band. East of that band the sea is dark and open. Far to the south rises Jan Mayen, crowned by the snowy volcano Beerenberg.
Q132868.w: Between Greenland and Svalbard: a white band of drifting pack ice along Greenland's coast, with open dark water to the east.
f: Beerenberg on Jan Mayen, 2,277 m high, is the northernmost active volcano on land.
Fram Strait, at its northern end, is the main gateway through which Arctic sea ice drifts out.
In winter its surface water sinks deep, helping to drive the Atlantic's circulation.

q.q: Through which strait does most ice leave the Arctic Ocean?

Q171510.t: Deep blue sea of the original Spice Islands
Q171510.s: The Banda Sea is ringed by a great curving arc of volcanic islands, and in places its floor drops to more than 7,000 m. Scattered in it are the tiny Banda Islands — for centuries the only place on Earth where nutmeg grew, a spice so valuable that European powers fought over these specks of land.
Q171510.w: Deep indigo sea in eastern Indonesia, rimmed by volcanic islands; look for tiny green specks and cones in the open water.
f: Under a 1667 treaty, England gave up its claim to Run, a tiny Banda nutmeg island, and kept Manhattan.
The Weber Deep, in the east of the sea, is more than 7 km deep.

q.q: Which spice once grew only on the Banda Islands?

Q41573.t: A stormy bay between France's straight coast and Spain
Q41573.s: Look east across the Bay of Biscay and you may see one of Europe's straightest coastlines: over 200 km of almost unbroken sand along France's Landes coast, with the Dune du Pilat piled up near its northern end. The southern shore is the opposite — Spain's green, mountainous north coast. The bay is famous for sudden storms and big Atlantic swell.
Q41573.w: A wide bay framed by France's long, straight sandy coast to the east and Spain's mountainous shore to the south.
f: The Dune du Pilat, about 100 m high, is the tallest sand dune in Europe.
Beyond the continental shelf its floor drops to more than 4,000 m.
Dolphins and whales feed here and are often seen from the ferries that cross it.

q.q: What is the tallest sand dune in Europe, on the Bay of Biscay?

Q165100.t: The strait between Africa and Madagascar
Q165100.s: This broad channel separates Madagascar from mainland Africa by at least 400 km of deep blue water. It opened more than 100 million years ago, as Madagascar drifted away from Africa. From above, look for the Zambezi's brown plume on the African side, and at the northern end the volcanic Comoros.
Q165100.w: Wide blue water between Mozambique's low coast and Madagascar's western shore; the Comoros islands mark its northern end.
f: Coelacanths, fish once thought extinct for 66 million years, live in deep water off the Comoros.
The channel is about 1,600 km long.
Humpback whales come here to breed during the southern winter.

q.q: Which “living fossil” fish lives off the Comoros?

Q41430.t: Where the equator meets the prime meridian
Q41430.s: Somewhere in this warm, hazy gulf lies 0° latitude, 0° longitude — the spot where the equator crosses the prime meridian, marked only by a weather buoy. To the north the Niger spreads into a vast delta of mangroves and creeks, and at night its oil and gas flares glow like embers. Offshore, volcanic islands rise from the sea.
Q41430.w: A broad, warm gulf off West Africa; the Niger Delta's green maze in the north, and volcanic islands such as Bioko offshore.
f: Bioko, São Tomé and Príncipe are volcanoes of the Cameroon Line, which runs from the mainland out to sea.
The Niger Delta is the largest river delta in Africa.
European sailors once named stretches of its shore the Gold Coast and the Ivory Coast.

q.q: Which two lines cross in the Gulf of Guinea?
x: Tropic of Cancer and prime meridian

Q545.t: A young, half-fresh sea born after the ice age
Q545.s: The Baltic is barely a sea at all: fed by more than 200 rivers and linked to the ocean only through the narrow Danish straits, its water is brackish, and in the far north almost fresh. It formed after the last ice age, and for a time it was a lake. Look for Gotland and Öland, long limestone islands off Sweden.
Q545.w: A large grey-blue inland sea in northern Europe; the long islands of Gotland and Öland lie off Sweden's south-east coast.
f: Most of the world's amber is found along its south-eastern shores.
In cold winters its northern gulfs freeze over completely.
Its average depth is only about 55 m.

q.q: What washes up on the Baltic's south-eastern shores?

Q45823.t: An Arctic sea kept half open by the Atlantic
Q45823.s: The Barents Sea is a sea of two halves. Warm Atlantic water keeps its south-western part open all winter — the port of Murmansk never freezes — while the north is locked in ice for much of the year. In August, plankton blooms can marble the water with milky turquoise, a sight satellites often capture.
Q45823.w: Open dark water in the south-west, pack ice in the north; the long, curved island of Novaya Zemlya walls it off in the east.
f: It is named after Willem Barentsz, who wintered on Novaya Zemlya in 1596–97.
Its waters hold one of the world's largest stocks of cod.
Svalbard, Franz Josef Land and Novaya Zemlya frame it to the west, north and east.

q.q: Why does Murmansk's port stay ice-free in winter?

Q1693.t: A shallow sea that was once dry land
Q1693.s: Much of the southern North Sea was dry land until about 8,000 years ago: hunters roamed a plain now called Doggerland, which joined Britain to the continent. Today the sea is shallow and busy. On clear days you may make out the regular grids of offshore wind farms and, along the Dutch, German and Danish coasts, the grey-brown tidal flats of the Wadden Sea.
Q1693.w: Grey-green shallow sea between Britain, Norway and the continent; tidal flats and barrier islands along the southern shore.
f: The Wadden Sea is the largest unbroken system of tidal flats in the world.
Its average depth is only about 95 m.
Trawlers still sometimes haul up mammoth bones from the Dogger Bank.

q.q: What is the drowned land under the southern North Sea called?

Q41735.t: Between Britain and Ireland, with Man in the middle
Q41735.s: Right in the middle of the Irish Sea sits the Isle of Man, green and hilly, with its own ancient parliament. On clear days you can pick out Anglesey and the mountains of Snowdonia to the east, Dublin Bay to the west, and wide bays where the ebbing tide uncovers kilometres of sand.
Q41735.w: A grey-green sea between Ireland and Britain; the Isle of Man near its centre, Anglesey off the Welsh coast.
f: The Isle of Man's parliament, Tynwald, traces its origins back more than a thousand years.
Morecambe Bay, on its English side, holds one of Britain's largest expanses of tidal sand and mud.
An old saying claims that from Snaefell, the Isle of Man's 621 m summit, you can see six kingdoms.

q.q: Which island sits near the middle of the Irish Sea?

Q49364.t: A shallow tropical sea over a drowned plain
Q49364.s: The Java Sea is remarkably shallow — on average less than 50 m deep — because it floods a former plain. In the ice ages, when sea levels were lower, you could have walked from Java to Borneo. Look for Jakarta's sprawl on the southern shore and, just offshore, the scatter of coral islets called the Thousand Islands.
Q49364.w: A warm, shallow, often greenish sea between Java and Borneo, busy with ships; Jakarta spreads along its southern shore.
f: The Thousand Islands off Jakarta actually number a little over a hundred.
Its seabed is part of the Sunda Shelf, one of the largest continental shelves on Earth.
Karimunjawa, a group of coral islands in its middle, is a national park.

q.q: In the ice ages, you could walk from Java to which island?

Q47632.t: Limestone towers, island chains and a lone volcano
Q47632.s: The Andaman Sea is framed by islands: the long Andaman and Nicobar chain in the west and, off Myanmar, the hundreds of forested isles of the Mergui Archipelago. Near Phuket, in Phang Nga Bay, sheer limestone towers rise straight out of green water. The Irrawaddy's muddy delta spreads across the north, staining the sea brown.
Q47632.w: Warm blue sea west of Thailand and Myanmar; island chains on both sides and brown river water in the north.
f: Barren Island, in its western part, is the only confirmed active volcano in South Asia.
The Mergui Archipelago off Myanmar counts some 800 islands.

q.q: Which river's delta spreads into the northern Andaman Sea?

Q37960.t: A sea tinted by the silt of China's rivers
Q37960.s: The name is no exaggeration: near the Chinese coast, silt from great rivers turns the water a murky yellow-brown that fades to green offshore. The Yellow Sea is shallow — about 44 m on average — and on the Korean side the tides are huge, retreating twice a day to bare kilometres of glistening mudflats.
Q37960.w: A shallow sea between China and Korea: yellow-brown water near the Chinese coast, broad grey mudflats along Korea's west.
f: At Incheon the tide can rise and fall by more than 8 m.
Its tidal flats are a vital stopover for millions of migrating shorebirds.
Near the island of Jindo, very low tides briefly expose a path of seabed almost 3 km long.

q.q: What gives the Yellow Sea its colour?

Q45341.t: Where the Yangtze pours into the Pacific
Q45341.s: At the mouth of the Yangtze, beside Shanghai, the East China Sea turns the colour of milky tea: Asia's longest river pours out a vast plume of silt. South of the city, look for the thin line of the Hangzhou Bay Bridge running some 36 km across the water. Farther east the sea deepens and clears towards the Ryukyu Islands.
Q45341.w: Brown water fanning out from the Yangtze mouth near Shanghai, turning blue-green offshore towards the Ryukyu chain.
f: The warm Kuroshio current runs north-east along its eastern edge.
Its wide continental shelf is mostly less than 200 m deep.
The Ryukyu Islands, strung out between Kyushu and Taiwan, form its eastern boundary.

q.q: Which great river empties into the East China Sea?

Q159252.t: The Arctic sea where the last mammoths lived
Q159252.s: North of the Bering Strait, the Chukchi Sea lies between Chukotka and Alaska, and the International Date Line runs straight through it — cross it and the calendar jumps a day. The sea is frozen for most of the year. On its western edge lies Wrangel Island, where woolly mammoths survived until roughly 4,000 years ago, long after they vanished elsewhere.
Q159252.w: Ice or dark open water north of the Bering Strait, between the hills of Chukotka and Alaska's flat north-west coast.
f: Wrangel Island is a UNESCO site and a major denning ground for polar bears.
In autumn, thousands of Pacific walruses haul out on its beaches.

q.q: Until roughly when did mammoths survive on Wrangel Island?

Q61304.t: The oil-rich southern pocket of the Gulf of Mexico
Q61304.s: Curving from Veracruz round to the Yucatán Peninsula, the Bay of Campeche is the Gulf of Mexico's southern pocket. Under its waters lies Cantarell, once one of the largest oil fields on Earth, and at night platform lights scatter across the sea. Along the southern shore, rivers spread into lagoons and mangrove-lined wetlands.
Q61304.w: The southern bight of the Gulf of Mexico, from Veracruz east to the Yucatán; platform lights offshore at night.
f: Laguna de Términos, on its southern shore, is Mexico's largest coastal lagoon.
Veracruz, on its western shore, was founded by Hernán Cortés in 1519.
The Grijalva and Usumacinta rivers reach it through a shared delta of swamps and channels.

q.q: Who founded Veracruz on the Bay of Campeche?

Q128880.t: A shallow sea over the land bridge to New Guinea
Q128880.s: Between northern Australia and New Guinea spreads the Arafura Sea — broad, warm and surprisingly shallow, mostly less than 80 m deep. In the ice ages it was dry land, and people and animals could walk between the two. From the air, look for green-brown water near the muddy coasts and the low, forested Aru Islands in the north.
Q128880.w: Wide, shallow, often greenish sea between Australia's Top End and New Guinea, with the low Aru Islands to the north.
f: The Gulf of Carpentaria opens off its southern side.
Torres Strait, a maze of islands and reefs, links it to the Coral Sea.

q.q: What did the Arafura Sea floor connect during the ice ages?

Q131418.t: A sea named after the “eastern” island
Q131418.s: The Timor Sea takes its name from Timor, and Timor's name comes from the Malay word for “east”. Most of it is a broad, shallow shelf off northern Australia, but close to Timor the floor plunges into a trough more than 3,000 m deep. On the Australian side, big tides wash in and out among rust-red cliffs and mangrove creeks.
Q131418.w: Open blue-green sea between the mountainous island of Timor and Australia's red Kimberley and Top End coasts.
f: The city of Darwin lies at its eastern edge.
Joseph Bonaparte Gulf, on its Australian side, is named after Napoleon's elder brother.

q.q: What does the Malay word behind the name “Timor” mean?

Q131217.t: A warm, shallow gulf ringed by tropical islands
Q131217.s: The Gulf of Thailand is warm and shallow — about 45 m deep on average — and its water often looks jade-green rather than blue. Look for the islands of Ko Samui and Ko Pha Ngan off the western shore, and the large island of Phu Quoc near the eastern one. At night, fishing boats' lamps can scatter the dark water with light.
Q131217.w: A broad, often greenish gulf south of Bangkok, with the Malay Peninsula to the west and scattered islands off both shores.
f: The Chao Phraya, the river of Bangkok, empties into its northern tip.
Its old name, the Gulf of Siam, is still used in some languages, including Russian.
Its seabed was dry land during the last ice age.

q.q: Which river of Bangkok flows into the Gulf of Thailand?

Q544914.t: Warm sea between India's tip and the coral atolls
Q544914.s: South-west of India lies a warm, bright-blue sea dotted with coral atolls. The Lakshadweep islands — the name means “a hundred thousand islands”, though there are only about three dozen — rise in its west, with the Maldives to the south. On the Indian side, look for the green, palm-lined Kerala coast with its maze of backwater lagoons.
Q544914.w: Bright blue water south-west of India, between the Kerala coast, Sri Lanka and the small ring-shaped atolls of Lakshadweep.
f: Kanyakumari, the southern tip of mainland India, looks out over it.
The Gulf of Mannar, between India and Sri Lanka, opens off its eastern side.
It is also known as the Lakshadweep Sea.

q.q: What does the name Lakshadweep mean?

Q183455.t: A remote icy sea off the Antarctic Peninsula
Q183455.s: Few people ever see the Bellingshausen Sea: it lies off the western side of the Antarctic Peninsula, far from regular shipping lanes. In winter it is a plain of pack ice; in summer, open water scattered with icebergs laps against ice shelves and the snowy mountains of Alexander Island, the largest island in Antarctica.
Q183455.w: Pack ice or iceberg-dotted water west of the Antarctic Peninsula, with the white bulk of Alexander Island to the east.
f: It is named after Fabian Gottlieb von Bellingshausen, whose Russian expedition sighted Antarctica in 1820.
The waters west of the Antarctic Peninsula are among the fastest-warming places on Earth.

q.q: Bellingshausen's 1820 expedition sailed for which country?

Q72154.t: Where West Antarctica's great glaciers meet the sea
Q72154.s: The Amundsen Sea is remote even by Antarctic standards, often choked with thick pack ice. Yet scientists watch it closely: two of the continent's biggest, fastest-changing glaciers, Thwaites and Pine Island, flow into it, and warm deep water is melting them from below. What happens here could raise sea levels around the world.
Q72154.w: Heavy pack ice and floating glacier tongues along the coast of West Antarctica, with nothing beyond but the ice sheet.
f: Thwaites Glacier is roughly as big as Great Britain.
The sea is named after Roald Amundsen, the first person to reach the South Pole, in 1911.

q.q: Which large glacier flows into the Amundsen Sea?

Q189262.t: The wide gateway between Greenland and Baffin Island
Q189262.s: Many transatlantic flights cross the Davis Strait, the wide channel between Greenland and Baffin Island. Even at its narrowest it is more than 300 km across. On the Greenland side, glaciers and bare rock line a fjord-cut coast; in spring and summer, icebergs drift south through the strait.
Q189262.w: Wide dark water between Greenland's glacier-cut west coast and the mountains of Baffin Island, often dotted with ice.
f: It is named after John Davis, an English navigator who sailed it in the 1580s.
Nuuk, Greenland's capital, lies on its eastern shore.
It links Baffin Bay in the north with the Labrador Sea in the south.

q.q: Which city lies on the Greenland shore of the Davis Strait?

Q33629.t: A frozen sea fed by two of Siberia's great rivers
Q33629.s: The Kara Sea is one of the coldest seas on Earth, iced over for most of the year. Two giant Siberian rivers, the Ob and the Yenisei, pour into it through estuaries hundreds of kilometres long, freshening its surface. To the west, the long mountain spine of Novaya Zemlya walls it off from the Barents Sea.
Q33629.w: Ice-covered sea north of western Siberia, between Novaya Zemlya and the Taymyr Peninsula; long river estuaries in the south.
f: The Gulf of Ob, the estuary of the Ob, reaches some 800 km inland.
It takes its name from the small Kara River, which flows into its south-western corner.
Severnaya Zemlya, on its eastern edge, was one of the last archipelagos to be mapped, in 1930–32.

q.q: Which two great rivers flow into the Kara Sea?

Q7988.t: The Arctic's ice factory, off the Lena Delta
Q7988.s: The Laptev Sea is one of the Arctic's great ice factories: offshore winds push ice away from the coast, the open water refreezes, and the new ice drifts off towards the pole. On its southern shore spreads the Lena Delta, the largest in the Arctic — in summer, a green fan laced with thousands of lakes and channels.
Q7988.w: Pack ice or grey water off northern Siberia; to the south, the huge fan of the Lena Delta, speckled with lakes.
f: It is named after the cousins Khariton and Dmitry Laptev, who charted this coast in the 1730s and 1740s.
The New Siberian Islands mark its eastern edge.

q.q: Which river's delta lies on the Laptev Sea?

Q186733.t: A huge bite out of Australia, edged by cliffs
Q186733.s: From the air, Australia's southern coast looks as if a giant bite was taken out of it: this is the Great Australian Bight. Along its head, the flat, treeless Nullarbor Plain ends abruptly in the Bunda Cliffs, pale walls of limestone that run unbroken for about 100 km above the dark ocean swell.
Q186733.w: A vast curve in Australia's southern coastline; look for a long, straight line of pale cliffs at the edge of a flat desert plain.
f: The Bunda Cliffs rise up to about 120 m straight out of the sea.
Southern right whales gather at the Head of Bight each winter to give birth.
Nullarbor comes from the Latin for “no tree”.

q.q: What does the name of the Nullarbor Plain mean?

Q44725.t: A rich, cold sea fenced by a chain of volcanoes
Q44725.s: Along its southern edge runs the Aleutian arc: a chain of volcanic islands, many topped with snowy cones, curving nearly 2,000 km towards Kamchatka and sealing off the Bering Sea. North of it lies one of the richest fishing grounds on Earth. In the ice ages its shallow northern part was dry land — the bridge by which people first reached the Americas.
Q44725.w: Wide grey-blue sea between Alaska and Russia's Far East, bounded in the south by the long chain of the Aleutian volcanoes.
f: It is named after Vitus Bering, a Danish navigator in Russian service who explored it in 1728.
The Pribilof Islands hold the largest breeding colony of northern fur seals.
In winter its sea ice can spread hundreds of kilometres south.

q.q: What was the Bering Sea's northern floor during the ice ages?

Q169274.t: The only sea without a single shore
Q169274.s: No coast bounds the Sargasso Sea: its edges are ocean currents, including the Gulf Stream, circling slowly around it. Inside that loop the water is warm, calm and startlingly clear and blue. Mats of golden-brown sargassum seaweed drift on the surface, and eels from rivers in Europe and North America swim thousands of kilometres here to spawn.
Q169274.w: Deep, clear blue open ocean east of Bermuda; on a calm day, streaks of golden-brown seaweed may show on the surface.
f: Bermuda lies on its western edge.
Its name comes from the Portuguese word for the floating seaweed.
Columbus's crews sailed through its weed in 1492 and feared they would run aground.

q.q: What forms the borders of the Sargasso Sea?

ne-lk-1159106739.t: The far eastern arm of Great Slave Lake
ne-lk-1159106739.s: McLeod Bay is the easternmost reach of Great Slave Lake's East Arm, a long corridor of dark, cold water between the rocky, cliff-lined shores of the Canadian Shield. Beyond its eastern tip the forest thins towards the treeless Barren Lands. The water here is clear and ice-bound for much of the year, and very few people live along its shores.
ne-lk-1159106739.w: A long, narrow arm of water at the eastern end of Great Slave Lake, with dark rocky shores and scattered islands.
f: At its eastern tip, the explorer George Back built Fort Reliance in 1833.
The Lockhart River flows into its eastern end.
Its shores lie within Thaidene Nëné, a national park reserve created in 2019.

q.q: Which lake is McLeod Bay part of?

Q736707.t: The small round lake between Huron and Erie
Q736707.s: Between the huge lakes Huron and Erie sits this small, roundish lake, a link in the chain. Its water arrives from the north through the St Clair River, which splits into a bird's-foot delta of marshes and channels, and leaves past Detroit down the Detroit River. For its size it is astonishingly shallow — about 3 m on average.
Q736707.w: A small round lake between Detroit and Ontario, with a fan of marshy delta channels on its north-eastern shore.
f: French explorers named it in 1679, on the feast day of Saint Clare.
A channel is dredged across it so that big lake freighters can pass.
Its delta, the St Clair Flats, is the largest delta in the Great Lakes system.

q.q: Which city lies on Lake Saint Clair's south-western shore?

Q202905.s: In the middle of southern Florida sits a nearly round lake so big it looks like a patch of sea — Okeechobee, “big water” in the Hitchiti language. It is remarkably shallow, under 3 m deep on average, and is ringed by a grassy dike. Historically its overflow spilled south as a slow sheet of water through the Everglades.
Q202905.w: A big, almost circular lake in south-central Florida, ringed by a levee, with green sugar-cane fields to the south.
f: It is the largest freshwater lake in Florida, covering about 1,900 km².
The Herbert Hoover Dike runs for about 230 km around it.
Canals link it to both the Atlantic and the Gulf of Mexico.

q.q: What does the name “Okeechobee” mean?

Q1640500.t: A lake that drains two ways at once
Q1640500.s: Wollaston Lake does something almost no lake does: it drains in two directions at once. One outlet, the Fond du Lac River, flows towards Lake Athabasca and on to the Mackenzie; the other, the Cochrane River, heads for Reindeer Lake and eventually Hudson Bay. It is the largest lake on Earth with two natural outlets like this.
Q1640500.w: A large, island-studded lake in north-eastern Saskatchewan, set in dark forest on the rocky Canadian Shield.
f: Water from its two outlets ends up thousands of kilometres apart — in the Beaufort Sea and in Hudson Bay.
Some of the world's richest uranium deposits lie near its shores.

q.q: What is unusual about Wollaston Lake?

Q965436.t: Alaska's largest lake, home to freshwater seals
Q965436.s: Iliamna is Alaska's largest lake, a long sheet of cold water between tundra hills and the volcanoes of the Aleutian Range. It holds a rare population of harbour seals that live in fresh water all year. Every summer millions of sockeye salmon swim up from Bristol Bay to spawn along its shores and streams, and in winter it freezes white.
Q965436.w: A long lake near the base of the Alaska Peninsula, with snowy volcanoes rising to the east.
f: Its water flows out through the Kvichak River into Bristol Bay.
Bristol Bay's sockeye salmon run is the largest in the world.
Local legend tells of “Illie”, a giant creature said to live in its depths.

q.q: Which unusual animals live in Iliamna Lake year-round?

Q169962.t: A deep, clear alpine lake high in the Sierra Nevada
Q169962.s: Lake Tahoe sits almost 1,900 m up in the Sierra Nevada, a deep blue oval ringed by pine forest and, for much of the year, snowy peaks. Its colour comes from depth and clarity: the lake drops to 501 m, and you can often see more than 20 m down into it. The California–Nevada border runs right through it.
Q169962.w: A deep-blue oval lake in the mountains west of Reno, surrounded by forest and snow-capped peaks.
f: It is the second-deepest lake in the United States, after Crater Lake.
The California–Nevada border bends at an angle in the middle of the lake.
Emerald Bay, on its south-western shore, is famous for its green-blue water.

q.q: Which two states share Lake Tahoe?

Q1801110.t: Wisconsin's big lake, beside a famous airshow town
Q1801110.s: Pilots know this lake: on its western shore lies Oshkosh, where each summer the EAA AirVenture fly-in fills the sky with thousands of aircraft, making its airport briefly one of the busiest on Earth. Lake Winnebago is the largest lake entirely within Wisconsin, and in winter anglers cut holes in its ice to spear giant lake sturgeon.
Q1801110.w: A large, oblong lake in eastern Wisconsin, with Oshkosh on the west shore and Fond du Lac at the southern tip.
f: It is shallow for its size, averaging only about 5 m deep.
The Fox River carries its water north to Green Bay and Lake Michigan.
A limestone ridge, part of the Niagara Escarpment, runs along its eastern shore.

q.q: Which famous aviation event takes place beside Lake Winnebago?

Q1132211.t: The largest lake on any island, astride the Arctic Circle
Q1132211.s: Nettilling Lake lies on Baffin Island, and no lake on any island in the world is larger. The Arctic Circle runs right across it, and ice covers it for most of the year. Its name comes from the Inuktitut word for the ringed seal — and seals do sometimes swim up into it from the sea.
Q1132211.w: A huge, irregular lake on the flat tundra of southern Baffin Island, white with ice for much of the year.
f: It covers about 5,500 km², roughly twice the size of Luxembourg.
It drains west through the Koukdjuak River into Foxe Basin.
