It is the largest lake in Nunavut.

q.q: What makes Nettilling Lake special?
q.a: The largest lake on any island

Q1262967.t: A remote tundra lake in Canada's Barren Lands
Q1262967.s: Dubawnt Lake lies deep in the Barren Lands, the treeless tundra west of Hudson Bay, far from any road or town. From above, look at the land around it: long, winding gravel ridges called eskers snake across the tundra, left by rivers that once flowed beneath the ice sheet. Ice often lingers on the lake itself into July.
Q1262967.w: A large, irregular lake on the bare tundra of southern Nunavut; look for long, winding esker ridges crossing the land.
f: In 1893 Joseph Tyrrell crossed the Barren Lands by canoe, travelling down the Dubawnt River.
Its water flows by the Dubawnt and Thelon rivers to Baker Lake and on to Hudson Bay.

q.q: What are the long, winding ridges around Dubawnt Lake?

Q1391737.t: A tundra lake near the very centre of Canada
Q1391737.s: Baker Lake sits almost at the geographic centre of Canada, on open tundra where the Thelon River ends its long journey from the west. On its shore stands the hamlet of Baker Lake, the only inland community in Nunavut and a well-known centre of Inuit art. Eastward, the long Chesterfield Inlet carries its water to Hudson Bay.
Q1391737.w: A broad lake on flat tundra west of Hudson Bay, joined to the bay by the long, narrow Chesterfield Inlet.
f: The hamlet's Inuktitut name, Qamani'tuaq, means roughly “where the river widens”.
Its artists are known worldwide for prints and colourful wall hangings.
Chesterfield Inlet runs for about 200 km from the lake to Hudson Bay.

q.q: What makes the hamlet of Baker Lake unique in Nunavut?
q.a: It is the only inland community

Q68467.t: A long valley lake between two mountain ranges
Q68467.s: Lake Champlain lies in a long valley like a blue ribbon, about 190 km from end to end, with the Adirondacks rising to the west and Vermont's Green Mountains to the east. Samuel de Champlain reached it in 1609 and gave it his name. It drains north: its water leaves through the Richelieu River into Quebec and the St Lawrence.
Q68467.w: A long, narrow north–south lake between the Adirondacks and the Green Mountains, with Burlington on its eastern shore.
f: In 1998 a US law briefly declared it a Great Lake; the label was dropped within weeks.
Local legend tells of “Champ”, a monster said to live in its depths.
Its northern tip reaches into Quebec.

q.q: What did a 1998 US law briefly declare Lake Champlain to be?

Q1089891.s: This long lake in north-western Saskatchewan is where the Churchill River begins its 1,600-km journey east to Hudson Bay. It is joined to its neighbour, Peter Pond Lake, by a narrow channel at the village of Buffalo Narrows. Around it spreads the boreal forest, a dark carpet broken by countless smaller lakes that flash in the sun.
Q1089891.w: A long lake in the forests of north-western Saskatchewan, joined at a narrow waist to Peter Pond Lake.
f: The Churchill River was a major highway of the fur trade, linking Hudson Bay with the far north-west.
The channel at Buffalo Narrows is called the Kisis Channel.

q.q: Where does the river flowing out of Churchill Lake end?

Q1516443.t: The “lake of the marten” in the northern forest
Q1516443.s: Lac la Martre — French for “lake of the marten” — sprawls across the forest north-west of Great Slave Lake, its shores ragged with bays and islands. The Tłı̨chǫ community of Whatì, whose name also means “marten lake”, stands on its shore. In winter the lake becomes a flat white plain; in summer, its dark water mirrors the sky.
Q1516443.w: A sprawling, many-bayed lake in the forest north-west of Great Slave Lake, scattered with islands.
f: Whatì was itself called Lac La Martre until 1996, when it took back its Tłı̨chǫ name.
In 2021 an all-season road reached Whatì for the first time.

q.q: Which animal is Lac la Martre named after?

Q12341531.t: Lake Superior's doorway to the Soo Locks
Q12341531.s: Whitefish Bay is the funnel at Lake Superior's eastern end: every freighter entering or leaving the lake passes through it, heading for the St Marys River and the Soo Locks at Sault Ste. Marie. From above, look for the sandy hook of Whitefish Point at its north-western tip, with the forested Ontario shore opposite.
Q12341531.w: A broad bay at the south-eastern corner of Lake Superior, between Michigan's Upper Peninsula and Ontario.
f: The lighthouse at Whitefish Point, first lit in 1849, is the oldest active light on Lake Superior.
In spring, thousands of migrating hawks and other birds funnel past Whitefish Point.

q.q: Which locks do ships head for after crossing Whitefish Bay?

Q2211837.t: The notch that gives Michigan's mitten its thumb
Q2211837.s: Look at Michigan from above and the Lower Peninsula really is shaped like a mitten — and Saginaw Bay is the gap between the thumb and the fingers. The bay is shallow and warms quickly in summer, when its water can turn greenish. The Saginaw River, draining the largest river basin in Michigan, empties into its head.
Q2211837.w: A long bay cutting south-west into Michigan from Lake Huron, between the Thumb and the rest of the Lower Peninsula.
f: Its inner part is only a few metres deep.
Its shores hold some of the largest coastal wetlands on the Great Lakes.

q.q: Saginaw Bay separates the rest of Michigan from which feature?

Q2000567.t: Lake Huron's sheltered channel behind Manitoulin
Q2000567.s: The North Channel is Lake Huron's quiet back room: a long, sheltered stretch of water tucked between Manitoulin Island and the rocky Ontario shore. Its coast is a maze of stony islands and coves loved by sailors. Near its eastern end, look for the La Cloche hills, whose white quartzite ridges can look like snow even in summer.
Q2000567.w: A long channel of Lake Huron between big Manitoulin Island and the mainland, with white-ridged hills near its eastern end.
f: Manitoulin Island, on its southern side, is the largest island in any freshwater lake.
Killarney Provincial Park protects the white quartzite ridges of the La Cloche Mountains.

q.q: Which island separates the North Channel from the rest of Lake Huron?

Q125309.t: A shallow Sahel lake that breathes with the rains
Q125309.s: Lake Chad is less a lake than a vast, shifting marsh at the edge of the Sahara. It is so shallow that its size swings with each rainy season, and since the 1960s it has shrunk to a fraction of its former extent. From above, look for a patchwork of open water, green reed beds and islands, fed from the south by the Chari River.
Q125309.w: A patchwork of open water, green marsh and sandy islands at the southern edge of the Sahara, where four countries meet.
f: The Chari River brings about 90% of its water.
Chad, Cameroon, Niger and Nigeria all border it.
Several thousand years ago a vast inland sea, known as Mega-Chad, spread across this basin.

q.q: Which river supplies most of Lake Chad's water?

Q503842.t: A turquoise lake with two names and marble caves
Q503842.s: This long lake reaches from the Andes out into the dry Patagonian steppe, its water a vivid glacial turquoise, and it answers to two names: General Carrera in Chile, Buenos Aires in Argentina. On its Chilean shore, waves have carved the Marble Caves, whose swirled stone reflects the blue water. It empties west through the Baker River, Chile's mightiest, to the Pacific.
Q503842.w: A long, vivid turquoise lake running east from the snowy Andes into the dry Patagonian steppe.
f: It is the largest lake in Chile.
The Marble Caves can be reached only by boat.

q.q: What is Lago General Carrera called in Argentina?

Q826464.t: A big blue lake beneath a perfect volcanic cone
Q826464.s: Look for Osorno: a snow-capped volcano so symmetrical it is often compared to Fuji, rising to 2,652 m above the eastern shore of Lake Llanquihue. Its neighbour Calbuco, rougher and broader, stands to the south-east. The lake itself is a broad blue sheet ringed by farmland, where German settlers arrived in the 1850s and founded towns such as Frutillar and Puerto Varas.
Q826464.w: A large, roundish blue lake in southern Chile, with the white cone of Osorno volcano on its eastern shore.
f: It is the second-largest lake in Chile.
Glaciers cap Osorno's summit all year round.

q.q: Which volcano rises on Lake Llanquihue's eastern shore?

Q31845950.t: A “suspended” lake held above the farmland by a dike
Q31845950.s: Hongze Lake sits higher than the towns and fields beside it: its water is held back by the old Gaojia Dike along its eastern shore. Some nine hundred years ago there was no big lake here at all. It grew after the Yellow River shifted south and choked the Huai River's route to the sea with silt, and engineers then raised the dike to store the Huai's water.
Q31845950.w: A broad, shallow, roughly rounded lake on the flat plain of northern Jiangsu, with a long dike along its eastern side.
f: It is one of China's five largest freshwater lakes.
The Huai River flows in from the west and leaves towards the Yangtze and the sea.

q.q: Why is Hongze called a “suspended” lake?
q.a: Its water sits above nearby land
x: It lies in a mountain crater

Q192215.t: Mongolia's “blue pearl”, little sister of Baikal
Q192215.s: Khövsgöl is a long, deep-blue lake in the mountains of northern Mongolia, some 200 km west of Baikal's southern tip — and in a sense its little sister, since its water flows out through the Egiin Gol and Selenga rivers into Baikal. It lies about 1,645 m up, fringed by larch forest, and in winter its ice is often more than a metre thick.
Q192215.w: A long north–south lake of deep blue among forested mountains near Mongolia's northern border, white with ice in winter.
f: It holds about 70% of Mongolia's fresh water.
Its deepest point is 262 m.

q.q: Into which famous lake does Khövsgöl's water eventually flow?

Q213769.t: Finland's deepest lake — and Helsinki's tap
Q213769.s: Päijänne is a long, narrow lake stretching north–south for about 120 km through the forests of central Finland. It is the country's deepest, and its clean water supplies Helsinki through a tunnel blasted 120 km through bedrock. In its southern part, look for Pulkkilanharju, a slender gravel ridge left by the ice age that carries a road across the water.
Q213769.w: A long, slender, island-dotted lake running north–south through central Finland, from Jyväskylä towards Lahti.
f: At about 95 m, it is the deepest lake in Finland.
The Päijänne Water Tunnel has carried water to the Helsinki region since 1982.
It is the second-largest lake in Finland, after Saimaa.

q.q: Which city gets its drinking water from Päijänne by tunnel?

Q504433.t: A lake on the long road of the Congo River
Q504433.s: Lake Mweru is one link in the vast chain of the Congo River system. At its southern end the Luapula River fans out into a swampy green delta; at the north, the Luvua carries the water on towards the Congo. The border between Zambia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo runs down the middle, and fishing villages line both shores.
Q504433.w: A broad lake on the Zambia–Congo border, with a green, swampy delta at its southern end.
f: David Livingstone reached its shores in 1867.
Its outflow, the Luvua, joins the Lualaba, as the upper Congo is called.

q.q: Which great river system does Lake Mweru belong to?

Q201843.t: A shallow border lake of lotus and cranes
Q201843.s: Lake Khanka is broad but astonishingly shallow — only a few metres deep — so the wind keeps its water a cloudy, sandy colour. The border between Russia and China crosses it, and on the Chinese side a narrow sand bar walls off a smaller companion lake. Its marshy shores hold nesting cranes and, in summer, pink lotus in bloom.
Q201843.w: A broad, pale, roundish lake on the Russia–China border north of Vladivostok, ringed by flat marshland.
f: Its water drains through the Sungacha River to the Ussuri and on to the Amur.
Wild lotus, rare this far north, blooms in its bays.
The wetlands around it are protected on both sides of the border.

q.q: Which two countries share Lake Khanka?

Q199938.t: The lake that swells as its river runs backwards
Q199938.s: Tonlé Sap does something extraordinary: each rainy season the Mekong rises so high that the river draining this lake reverses and flows back into it. The lake swells to several times its dry-season size, drowning forests and fields in brown water. Floating villages rise and fall with it, and the temples of Angkor lie just north of its shore.
Q199938.w: A large, brown, shallow lake in the heart of Cambodia; much larger in the wet season, with flooded forest around it.
f: Its fish are a main source of protein for millions of Cambodians.
In the dry season much of it is only about a metre deep.
Each autumn Cambodia's Water Festival marks the moment the river turns back towards the Mekong.

q.q: What happens to the Tonlé Sap River in the rainy season?

Q1144905.t: The shallow southern end of the Peipus lake system
Q1144905.s: Three lakes stand in a row here: huge Lake Peipus in the north, the narrow Lämmijärv in the middle and, at the southern end, Lake Pskov — Pihkva in Estonian. The Estonia–Russia border crosses it. The lake is shallow, under 4 m on average, and freezes over in winter; the Velikaya River flows in after passing the old city of Pskov.
Q1144905.w: A shallow lake south of the huge Lake Peipus, joined to it by a narrow strait; the Velikaya delta at its south-eastern corner.
f: Together with Lake Peipus, it forms one of the largest lakes in Europe.
The small Talabsk Islands in its middle hold old fishing villages.

q.q: Which larger lake is Lake Pskov joined to?

ne-lk-1159113481.t: A Karelian lake at the cradle of the Kalevala
ne-lk-1159113481.s: Sredneye Kuito — “Middle Kuito” — is the central link in a chain of three lakes stretching some 140 km across the forests of northern Karelia, filling long cracks in the ancient bedrock. On its northern shore stands the settlement of Kalevala, called Ukhta until 1963. In the villages around here, Elias Lönnrot collected many of the old songs he wove into the Finnish epic Kalevala.
ne-lk-1159113481.w: A long, island-studded lake among the dark forests of northern Karelia, part of a chain of lakes running west to east.
f: Its water flows east through Lower Kuito into the Kem River and on to the White Sea.
The Kuito lakes are tectonic: they fill cracks in the Earth's crust.

q.q: Which epic is linked to the villages around the Kuito lakes?

Q184492.t: The sea bay that became a lake as Sweden rose
Q184492.s: Mälaren is a sprawling lake of bays and islands stretching about 120 km west from Stockholm. A thousand years ago it was still an arm of the Baltic; as the land slowly rose after the ice age, it was cut off and turned fresh. Stockholm grew up exactly where lake meets sea, and the city's islands scatter across the water at the lake's eastern end.
Q184492.w: A long, branching lake of bays and wooded islands running west from Stockholm, with the city's islands at its eastern end.
f: Birka, a Viking-age trading town on the island of Björkö, is a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Drottningholm, home of the Swedish royal family, stands on one of its islands.
It supplies drinking water to Stockholm and the surrounding region.

q.q: What was Mälaren a thousand years ago?
q.a: An arm of the Baltic Sea

Q216621.t: A steppe lake where the Irtysh sets off on its long trip
Q216621.s: Water that enters Lake Zaysan is at the start of a very long journey: the Black Irtysh flows in from China and leaves as the Irtysh, bound for the Ob and the Arctic Ocean. The lake lies in a broad basin in eastern Kazakhstan, with the Altai to the north and the Saur and Tarbagatai ranges to the south. Since the 1960s a dam downstream has raised its level.
Q216621.w: A broad, elongated lake in the steppe of eastern Kazakhstan, between the Altai and the Saur–Tarbagatai ranges.
f: The Bukhtarma Dam on the Irtysh has held its level higher since the 1960s, making it part of a vast reservoir.
It freezes over for several months every winter.

q.q: Which river flows out of Lake Zaysan?

Q1640519.t: A desert basin filled to keep Baghdad dry
Q1640519.s: Lake Tharthar is a lake by design. It fills a natural depression in the desert between the Tigris and the Euphrates, and since the 1950s engineers have diverted the Tigris's floodwater into it to protect Baghdad downstream. From above it's a large sheet of blue in the tan desert, its shores bare and pale.
Q1640519.w: A large blue lake in the desert north-west of Baghdad, between the Tigris and the Euphrates.
f: It is the largest lake in Iraq.
A canal from the Tigris near Samarra feeds it.
Other canals can send its water on to the Euphrates.

q.q: Why was Tigris water diverted into Lake Tharthar?

Q756106.t: The “Eye of Quebec”: a ring lake in an ancient crater
Q756106.s: Few lakes are as unmistakable from the air: a near-perfect ring of water about 70 km across, circling a huge island. It marks an impact crater blasted by an asteroid around 214 million years ago and worn down ever since. The ring filled to its present size after a dam was built in the 1960s, earning it the nickname “the Eye of Quebec”.
Q756106.w: An unmistakable ring of water around a large, round island in the forests of eastern Quebec.
f: The Daniel-Johnson Dam, which raised the lake, is the largest multiple-arch-and-buttress dam in the world.
Astronauts often photograph it — the ring is easy to spot from orbit.

q.q: What formed the Manicouagan ring?

Q1638191.t: A white salt lake in the heart of the Western Desert
Q1638191.s: In the red sand country of Western Australia's deserts, Kumpupintil shows up as a vast white pan, glaring under the sun and usually dry. Its English name, Lake Disappointment, dates from 1897, when the explorer Frank Hann followed creeks here hoping for fresh water and found salt. For the Martu people, whose country this is, it is a place of great significance.
Q1638191.w: A large white salt pan dotted with dark islands, surrounded by dune desert in inland Western Australia.
f: The Canning Stock Route, one of the world's most remote tracks, passes nearby.
After rare heavy rains, shallow water can spread across it for months.

q.q: Why did Frank Hann name it Lake Disappointment?
q.a: He found salt, not fresh water
x: It was smaller than on his map

Q1074063.t: A glittering salt lake on the WA–NT border
Q1074063.s: From cruise height Lake Mackay looks like a giant white stain spilled across red desert, its edges lacy with inlets and its surface dotted with small islands. It is one of Australia's largest salt lakes, yet most years it holds little or no water. The ruler-straight border between Western Australia and the Northern Territory runs right across it.
Q1074063.w: A huge, ragged white salt pan in the red dune desert where Western Australia meets the Northern Territory.
f: The Pintupi people call it Wilkinkarra.
It is named after explorer Donald Mackay, who reached it in 1930 and was among the first to cycle around Australia.
It covers about 3,500 km² and is roughly 100 km across.

q.q: What do the Pintupi people call Lake Mackay?

Q965973.t: A dazzling salt pan where racers chase speed
Q965973.s: Lake Gairdner is a salt pan some 160 km long, so white it can hurt the eyes, lying at the northern foot of the rust-red Gawler Ranges. Its crust is more than a metre thick in places, hard and flat enough that each year drivers and riders come to race across it during Speed Week, chasing records on the salt.
Q965973.w: A long, dazzling white salt lake in South Australia, just north of the reddish Gawler Ranges.
f: It lies within Lake Gairdner National Park.
It is South Australia's third-largest salt lake, after Eyre and Torrens.

q.q: Why do racers come to Lake Gairdner?

Q163855.t: A long salt lake that almost never fills
Q163855.s: Lake Torrens runs as a long, pale streak along the western foot of the Flinders Ranges, a salt pan that has filled with water only a handful of times in recorded history. Early colonial explorers, seeing it from the hills, imagined a vast horseshoe of salt lakes barring the way north — a belief that held for years.
Q163855.w: A long, narrow white salt pan running north–south just west of the rugged Flinders Ranges in South Australia.
f: It is named after Robert Torrens, chairman of the commission that founded the colony of South Australia.
It is South Australia's second-largest salt lake, after Kati Thanda–Lake Eyre.
The lake and its shores form Lake Torrens National Park.

q.q: Which mountain range rises just east of Lake Torrens?

Q626907.t: A salt pan between the Flinders Ranges and red dunes
Q626907.s: On the far side of the Flinders Ranges from Lake Torrens lies its twin: Lake Frome, a flat white salt pan about 100 km long. To its west rise the rugged ridges of the northern Flinders; to its east, lines of red sand dunes march away into the Strzelecki Desert. Water covers it only after rare heavy rains.
Q626907.w: A long white salt pan east of the northern Flinders Ranges, bordered on the east by parallel red dunes.
f: It is named after Edward Frome, Surveyor-General of South Australia in the 1840s.
The Arkaroola wilderness sanctuary lies in the ranges just to its west.

q.q: Which desert's red dunes border Lake Frome to the east?

ne-lk-1159126435.t: A super-salty lagoon behind a ribbon of sand
ne-lk-1159126435.s: Along the coast of Tamaulipas, a thin ribbon of sandy barrier islands runs for well over 100 km, and behind it lies Laguna Madre: a long, shallow lagoon that is saltier than the sea, because little fresh water flows in and the sun evaporates much of it. In winter it teems with ducks, including a large share of the world's redheads.
ne-lk-1159126435.w: A long, shallow, greenish lagoon on Mexico's Gulf coast south of the Rio Grande, walled off from the sea by thin sandy islands.
f: It is one of the few hypersaline coastal lagoons in the world.
The Rio Grande delta separates it from its twin, the Laguna Madre of Texas.

q.q: Why is Laguna Madre saltier than the sea?

Q503301.t: An accidental lake in a desert below sea level
Q503301.s: The Salton Sea is an accident. In 1905 the Colorado River burst through an irrigation canal and poured into this desert basin for almost two years, creating California's largest lake. Its surface lies about 70 m below sea level, and with no outlet it has grown saltier than the Pacific. Look for green farm fields crowding its southern shore.
Q503301.w: A long blue lake in the desert south-east of Palm Springs, with the green grid of the Imperial Valley to the south.
f: It is a vital stop for migrating birds on the Pacific Flyway.
As it shrinks, it exposes wide, pale bands of dried lake bed.

q.q: How did the Salton Sea form in 1905–1907?
q.a: The Colorado River broke into it

Q4121.t: A sea turned into a lake by one long dam
Q4121.s: Until 1932 this was the Zuiderzee, a stormy arm of the North Sea. Then the Afsluitdijk, a dam 32 km long, sealed it off, and the salt water slowly turned fresh. From above, the dam is a razor-straight line across the water, and to the east and south lie Flevoland's polders — ruler-drawn fields on what was once the seabed.
Q4121.w: A broad, grey-green lake in the Netherlands, closed off from the Wadden Sea in the north by a long, perfectly straight dam.
f: Flevoland, built on land reclaimed from it, became the youngest Dutch province in 1986.
It is one of the largest freshwater lakes in Western Europe.
A second dam, the Houtribdijk, splits off its southern part, the Markermeer.

q.q: What was the IJsselmeer before 1932?

ne-lk-1159126643.t: The pink lagoons of the “Rotten Sea”
ne-lk-1159126643.s: Few sights from the air are stranger than Syvash: a maze of shallow lagoons between Crimea and the mainland, streaked pink, rust-red and milky green. The water is so salty that salt-loving algae tint it, and in summer heat it smells — hence its other name, the Rotten Sea. To the east, the thin Arabat Spit seals it off from the Sea of Azov.
ne-lk-1159126643.w: A maze of pink, red and green lagoons between Crimea and the mainland, fenced off from the Sea of Azov by a thin spit.
f: The Arabat Spit, which separates it from the Sea of Azov, is about 110 km long.
Much of it is less than a metre deep.
Salt has been gathered along its shores for centuries.

q.q: What gives Syvash its pink and red colours?

Q182719.t: The Jade Sea in the desert of northern Kenya
Q182719.s: Lake Turkana is called the Jade Sea: in the right light, algae turn its water a striking green against the brown lava desert around it. It is the largest permanent lake in any desert, and its shores have yielded some of the most important fossils of early humans. Volcanic islands with crater lakes rise from its middle.
Q182719.w: A long, narrow green-blue lake in the barren north of Kenya, reaching north into Ethiopia, with dark volcanic islands.
f: The Omo River, flowing in from Ethiopia, brings almost all of its water.
The skeleton of “Turkana Boy”, about 1.5 million years old, was found near its western shore in 1984.
Its old name, Lake Rudolf, was given in 1888 in honour of Crown Prince Rudolf of Austria.

q.q: What is Lake Turkana's nickname?

Q5605.t: A shallow lagoon behind a long ribbon of dunes
Q5605.s: Look for a long, slender sand spit, crested with forest and dunes, running parallel to the Baltic coast — and behind it a shallow, brownish-green lagoon. The Vistula Lagoon is on average less than 3 m deep, and its natural link to the sea is a single narrow strait at Baltiysk. At its eastern end, the Pregolya River flows in from Kaliningrad.
Q5605.w: A long, shallow lagoon along the Baltic coast near Kaliningrad, cut off from the sea by a thin wooded spit.
f: The Vistula Spit that shelters it runs for about 65 km.
In winter the lagoon often freezes over.
Its water is brackish, a mix of river water and the Baltic.

q.q: Which city stands on the river entering the lagoon's eastern end?

Q81150.t: Mongolia's biggest lake, a salty oval in the steppe
Q81150.s: Uvs Nuur is Mongolia's largest lake: a broad, salty oval in a closed basin where desert dunes, steppe, taiga and snowy peaks all lie within sight of one another. No river flows out. Winters here are bitterly cold and the lake stays frozen for months; in summer, its blue shimmers against the brown steppe.
Q81150.w: A large, oval, salty lake in the dry steppe of north-western Mongolia, ringed by the mountains of its basin.
f: The Uvs Nuur Basin, shared with Russia's Tuva, is a UNESCO World Heritage site.
It lies about 750 m above sea level, at the lowest point of its basin.

q.q: Uvs Nuur is the largest lake in which country?

Q201294.t: China's largest lake, blue on the high plateau
Q201294.s: At about 3,200 m on the edge of the Tibetan Plateau lies China's largest lake, a vast salty sheet of vivid blue. Its Chinese name, Qinghai, means “blue sea”, and the Mongolian name Kokonor means “blue lake” — the whole province is named after it. In July its shores glow with yellow rapeseed fields, framed by bare brown mountains.
Q201294.w: A huge, bright blue oval lake on the high, bare north-eastern edge of the Tibetan Plateau, west of Xining.
f: Bird Island is a nesting ground for bar-headed geese, famous for flying over the Himalayas.
Its water is salty, though less so than the sea.
The Qinghai–Tibet Railway runs along its northern shore.

q.q: What does the Mongolian name Kokonor mean?

Q2007652.t: The “Lake of Salt” west of Karbala
Q2007652.s: Lake Milh — Buhayrat al-Milh, the “Lake of Salt” — spreads across a desert depression west of Karbala. Floodwater from the Euphrates reaches it by canal via Lake Habbaniyah, but in recent decades it has shrunk sharply, leaving wide white salt flats around a smaller sheet of blue-green water. It is also known as Lake Razzaza.
Q2007652.w: A shallow blue-green lake ringed by white salt flats in the desert west of Karbala, south-west of Baghdad.
f: It is one of the largest lakes in Iraq.
As its water shrank, it grew too salty for most fish.

q.q: What does Buhayrat al-Milh mean?

Q204703.t: A stormy sea ringed by a loop of sub-Antarctic islands
Q204703.s: The Scotia Sea is one of the stormiest stretches of water on Earth, swept by the Antarctic Circumpolar Current and dotted with icebergs. Its edges are traced by the Scotia Arc, a great loop of islands from South Georgia to the South Shetlands. In 1916 Ernest Shackleton crossed it in a small open boat to fetch help for his stranded crew.
Q204703.w: Grey, wind-whipped open ocean between South America and Antarctica, with icebergs and the snowy peaks of South Georgia.
f: It is named after the Scotia, ship of the Scottish National Antarctic Expedition of 1902–04.
Shackleton's boat journey from Elephant Island to South Georgia covered more than 1,200 km.
Its cold waters swarm with Antarctic krill, food for whales and penguins.

q.q: What did Shackleton cross the Scotia Sea in, in 1916?

Q41837.t: The seaway between Arabia and the Horn of Africa
Q41837.s: The Gulf of Aden is a long wedge of deep blue between the bare mountains of Yemen and the dry coast of Somalia. Ships heading to and from the Suez Canal funnel through it. Beneath it runs a spreading ridge where Arabia and Africa are slowly pulling apart. At its eastern mouth lies Socotra, an island of strange, umbrella-shaped dragon's blood trees.
Q41837.w: A long, deep-blue gulf between Yemen's rugged coast and the Horn of Africa, narrowing west towards the Bab-el-Mandeb strait.
f: The Bab-el-Mandeb strait at its western end is only about 30 km wide.
Socotra and its unique plants are a UNESCO World Heritage site.

q.q: Which famous trees grow on Socotra, off the Gulf of Aden?

Q79948.t: Gateway to the Gulf, beneath the Hajar Mountains
Q79948.s: The Gulf of Oman is the entrance hall to the Persian Gulf: tankers file through it towards the Strait of Hormuz. Along its south-western shore, the jagged, rust-brown Hajar Mountains drop almost straight into the sea, with Muscat tucked between them. In the north-west, the Musandam Peninsula frays into fjords that earned it the nickname “Norway of Arabia”.
Q79948.w: A wide gulf between Oman's rugged mountain coast and Iran, narrowing north-west towards the Strait of Hormuz.
f: Tankers carrying a large share of the world's oil pass through it every day.
Musandam is an exclave of Oman, cut off from the rest of the country by the UAE.

q.q: Which peninsula is nicknamed the “Norway of Arabia”?

Q38882.t: A volcanic sea between Italy and its great islands
Q38882.s: The Tyrrhenian is ringed by volcanoes and islands: Italy's west coast, Corsica, Sardinia and Sicily enclose it. Above the Bay of Naples rises Vesuvius, and in the south the Aeolian Islands include Stromboli, which throws up small bursts of lava every few minutes. On a night flight, you might even catch its red glow.
Q38882.w: A deep-blue sea west of mainland Italy, framed by Corsica and Sardinia; volcanic islands north of Sicily.
f: Its name comes from the Tyrrhenians, as the ancient Greeks called the Etruscans.
Sailors have long called Stromboli the “Lighthouse of the Mediterranean”.
Its deepest point lies about 3,800 m down.

q.q: Which volcano is known as the “Lighthouse of the Mediterranean”?

Q44133.t: Russia's northern inland sea, white for half the year
Q44133.s: The White Sea cuts deep into northern Russia, a branching inland sea that lives up to its name: it is covered with ice for about half the year. Near its western shores lie the Solovetsky Islands, where a monastery founded in the 15th century still stands. In the south-east, the Northern Dvina splits into a delta around Arkhangelsk, once Russia's chief seaport.
Q44133.w: A branching inland sea in Russia's far north, white with ice in winter; the Solovetsky Islands near its western shores.
f: The Solovetsky Islands are a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Tides in its Mezen Bay can reach about 10 m.
The White Sea–Baltic Canal links it to Lake Onega and the Baltic.

q.q: Which city stands at the Northern Dvina delta on the White Sea?

Q223810.t: Hudson Bay's shallow, river-fed southern pocket
Q223810.s: James Bay is the shallow southern pocket of Hudson Bay, fed by so many big rivers that its water is only mildly salty. Its shores are low and flat — a wide fringe of marsh and tidal mudflats where huge flocks of geese and shorebirds stop on migration. In winter it freezes over completely, and the frozen coast blurs into the white land beyond.
Q223810.w: A shallow bay at the southern end of Hudson Bay, between Ontario and Quebec, with low, marshy shores and many river mouths.
f: It is named after Captain Thomas James, who explored it in 1631.
Moose Factory, a Hudson's Bay Company post founded in 1673, stands near its southern shore.
Akimiski, its largest island, is part of Nunavut.

q.q: James Bay is the southern extension of which body of water?

Q180844.t: Home of the Morning Glory roll clouds
Q180844.s: In September and October, glider pilots travel to the southern shore of the Gulf of Carpentaria for a rare sight: the Morning Glory, a tube-shaped roll cloud that can stretch for hundreds of kilometres and rolls in at dawn. The gulf itself is a broad, shallow, warm sea between Cape York and Arnhem Land, fringed with mangroves and mudflats.
Q180844.w: A huge, squarish bay in northern Australia, between Cape York Peninsula and Arnhem Land; muddy green near the coasts.
f: It is named after Pieter de Carpentier, a governor-general of the Dutch East Indies.
Most of it is less than 70 m deep.
The Morning Glory is best seen near the small town of Burketown.

q.q: What is the Morning Glory over the Gulf of Carpentaria?

Q132811.t: The long sea behind Baja California
Q132811.s: Look for a long, narrow sea between the bare mountains of the Baja California peninsula and mainland Mexico — about 1,100 km from end to end. It opened as Baja slowly tore away from the continent along the San Andreas fault system. Its water is famously rich in life; Jacques Cousteau called it “the aquarium of the world”.
Q132811.w: A long, narrow blue sea between the desert mountains of Baja California and mainland Mexico, dotted with bare islands.
f: The vaquita, the world's smallest porpoise, lives only in its northern end.
Its islands and protected areas are a UNESCO World Heritage site.
It is also called the Sea of Cortés.

q.q: Which tiny, rare animal lives only in the Gulf of California?

Q207702.t: The icy gateway into Hudson Bay
Q207702.s: Every ship bound for Hudson Bay from the Atlantic must pass through this long, icy strait between Baffin Island and northern Quebec. Henry Hudson sailed it in 1610. Its tides are fierce: in Ungava Bay, on its southern side, the sea can rise and fall by more than 15 m. For much of the year, drifting pack ice fills it from shore to shore.
Q207702.w: A long, wide strait between Baffin Island's rugged south coast and Quebec's Ungava Peninsula, often full of drifting ice.
f: It is about 750 km long.
Ungava Bay has some of the highest tides on Earth.

q.q: Which bay on the Hudson Strait has some of the world's highest tides?

Q34640.t: The narrow, busy sea between England and France
Q34640.s: At its narrowest, the Strait of Dover, only about 33 km separate England from France — on a clear day the white chalk cliffs on both sides are easy to pick out. It is one of the busiest shipping lanes on Earth; look for the white wakes of ships lined up like traffic. Beneath the seabed, the Channel Tunnel links the two coasts.
Q34640.w: A long sea narrowing eastwards between England's south coast and northern France, busy with ships; chalk cliffs at the Dover end.
f: The Channel Tunnel, opened in 1994, runs for about 38 km beneath the sea.
About 450,000 years ago a huge ice-age flood broke through a chalk ridge here, helping to cut Britain off.
The French call it La Manche, “the sleeve”.

q.q: About how wide is the Strait of Dover at its narrowest?

Q795608.t: Turquoise cays where three countries meet the Caribbean
Q795608.s: The Gulf of Honduras is a sheltered corner of the Caribbean where the coasts of Belize, Guatemala and Honduras meet. Scattered across it are low mangrove cays and the southern tip of the great Mesoamerican Barrier Reef, bright turquoise against the deep blue. Rivers from the green mountains inland tint the water brown near their mouths.
Q795608.w: A broad Caribbean inlet south of Belize, with turquoise reefs and small cays; the Bay Islands of Honduras lie to the east.
f: Whale sharks, the largest fish on Earth, visit the waters off Utila in the Bay Islands.
Belize's Sapodilla Cayes, near its mouth, mark the southern end of the barrier reef.
The Motagua River from Guatemala empties into it.

q.q: Which three countries share the shores of the Gulf of Honduras?

Q122574.t: A nearly fresh northern gulf where the land still rises
Q122574.s: The Gulf of Bothnia is the Baltic's long northern arm between Sweden and Finland, and its water is so fresh that in the far north it is barely salty. Each winter ice spreads across it, and in some years it freezes from shore to shore. The land here is still rising after the ice age, adding new islets and skerries to the Kvarken archipelago every century.
Q122574.w: A long grey-blue gulf between Sweden and Finland, white with ice in winter; an island-strewn narrow waist at Kvarken.
f: Sweden's High Coast has risen about 286 m since the ice sheet melted — more than anywhere else known.
The High Coast and the Kvarken archipelago form a joint UNESCO World Heritage site.
Around Kvarken the land still rises by up to about 8 mm a year.

q.q: Why do new islands keep appearing in the Gulf of Bothnia?

Q13924.t: A long blue sea between Italy and a coast of islands
Q13924.s: The Adriatic stretches for about 800 km between Italy's smooth coastline and the Balkans' jagged one. On the eastern side, the Croatian shore dissolves into long islands lying parallel to the coast — more than a thousand of them, counting islets and reefs. In the north the sea is shallow and greenish, with the Po delta and the lagoon of Venice on its western side.
Q13924.w: A long sea between Italy and the Balkans; the Croatian coast breaks into rows of long islands parallel to the shore.
f: The Bora, a fierce cold wind, can sweep down from the mountains onto its eastern coast.
Its name comes from the ancient port of Adria, near the Po delta.
The Strait of Otranto, about 70 km wide, links it to the Ionian Sea.

q.q: Which ancient port gave the Adriatic Sea its name?

Q81136.t: The legendary sea route through the Arctic islands
Q81136.s: For centuries sailors dreamed of a shortcut from Europe to Asia over the top of North America. The Northwest Passage is that route: a maze of channels threading between the frozen islands of the Canadian Arctic. From above it's white ice cracked into floes, with dark open lanes in late summer. Roald Amundsen was the first to sail it, in 1903–06.
Q81136.w: Ice-choked channels winding between the brown and white islands of the Canadian Arctic; open water only in late summer.
f: Amundsen's ship, the Gjøa, was a small former herring boat.
In 1944 the Canadian police schooner St. Roch became the first ship to cross it in a single season.
There are several possible routes, depending on where the ice allows a passage.

q.q: Who first sailed the Northwest Passage, in 1903–06?

Q37495.t: The deepest part of the Mediterranean
Q37495.s: Between the heel of Italy and the west coast of Greece lies the Ionian Sea, a clear, deep-blue expanse. Off Greece's south-western coast the floor plunges to about 5,270 m — the deepest point of the whole Mediterranean. Along its eastern side, look for the green, mountainous Ionian Islands: Corfu, Kefalonia and Zakynthos, fringed with pale cliffs.
Q37495.w: Deep-blue sea between southern Italy, Sicily and western Greece, with the green Ionian Islands along the Greek side.
f: Loggerhead sea turtles nest on the beaches of Zakynthos.
One Greek legend links its name to Io, who swam across it.
The Strait of Otranto links it to the Adriatic in the north.

q.q: About how deep is the Mediterranean's deepest point, in the Ionian Sea?

Q169523.t: A northern sea of red-cliffed islands and winter ice
Q169523.s: The Gulf of St Lawrence is where the Great Lakes' water finally meets the Atlantic — a broad inland sea ringed by Quebec, the Maritime provinces and Newfoundland. Look for Prince Edward Island's red cliffs and green fields, and the long, low Anticosti Island. In late winter, drifting pack ice fills much of the gulf, and harp seals give birth on it.
Q169523.w: A broad gulf east of Quebec; the crescent of Prince Edward Island in the south, long Anticosti Island in the north.
f: Jacques Cartier sailed into it in 1534.
Anticosti Island is larger than the whole province of Prince Edward Island.
The Magdalen Islands, near its centre, are strung together by long sand dunes.

q.q: Which animals give birth on the gulf's pack ice in late winter?

Q185291.t: A sea squeezed between two volcanic arcs
Q185291.s: The Molucca Sea is being swallowed from both sides: the sea floor beneath it is sinking under two volcanic arcs at once, a rare arrangement geologists call double subduction. Look for perfect volcanic cones rising from the water, like Ternate and Tidore off Halmahera — islands where cloves originally grew.
Q185291.w: Deep-blue sea between Sulawesi's long northern arm and Halmahera, dotted with steep volcanic cone islands.
f: Cloves originally grew on only a handful of islands here, including Ternate and Tidore.
The equator runs right across it.

q.q: Which spice originally grew on Ternate and Tidore?

Q199436.t: A volcanic sea framed by the Bismarck Archipelago
Q199436.s: The Bismarck Sea is enclosed by a great arc of islands — New Britain, New Ireland and the Admiralty Islands — with the north coast of New Guinea to the south. Volcanoes rise along its edges, among them Manam, a near-perfect cone just off the mainland. Where the Sepik River meets the sea, its brown plume spreads into the blue.
Q199436.w: Deep-blue sea north of New Guinea, ringed by the long, mountainous islands of New Britain and New Ireland.
f: It was named after Otto von Bismarck when the region became a German colony in the 1880s.
Manam, a volcano island off New Guinea, is one of the most active volcanoes in the region.

q.q: Which river's brown plume spreads into the Bismarck Sea?

Q199479.t: A deep tropical sea between New Guinea and the Solomons
Q199479.s: Framed by New Guinea's long eastern tail, the mountainous island of New Britain and the Solomon Islands, the Solomon Sea is warm, deep and dotted with coral islands. Along its northern edge, the New Britain Trench drops to more than 8,000 m. In the west lie the low, flat Trobriand Islands, ringed with turquoise reefs.
Q199479.w: Deep-blue sea east of New Guinea's tail, bounded by New Britain to the north and the Solomon Islands to the east.
f: The Trobriand Islands became world-famous through the anthropologist Bronisław Malinowski, who lived there in the 1910s.
Its warm waters lie within the Coral Triangle, one of the richest reef regions on Earth.

q.q: Which anthropologist made the Trobriand Islands famous?

Q48359.t: The narrow sea lane that links two oceans
Q48359.s: This long funnel of water between Sumatra and the Malay Peninsula links the Indian Ocean with the Pacific, and tens of thousands of ships squeeze through it every year. Look for their wakes, often in long lines. Near Singapore, where it meets the Singapore Strait, the shipping channel narrows to less than 3 km. The strait takes its name from Malacca, once a great trading city.
Q48359.w: A long, narrowing strait between Sumatra's forested coast and the Malay Peninsula, streaked with the wakes of many ships.
f: It is about 900 km long.
In the 15th century the Sultanate of Malacca controlled the trade passing through it.

q.q: Which two land masses does the Strait of Malacca separate?

Q194477.t: The invisible line between Asian and Australian wildlife
Q194477.s: Down the middle of the Makassar Strait, between Borneo and Sulawesi, runs an invisible boundary: the Wallace Line. In the 1850s Alfred Russel Wallace noticed how different the animals on either side were — mostly Asian species to the west, more and more Australasian ones to the east. The strait is deep, and most of the Pacific water flowing through Indonesia into the Indian Ocean passes through it.
Q194477.w: A wide, deep strait between Borneo's green coast and the spidery outline of Sulawesi.
f: Deep water here kept Borneo and Sulawesi apart even when ice-age sea levels were low.
Makassar, on Sulawesi's south-western coast, has been a major port for centuries.

q.q: Which famous biological boundary runs through the Makassar Strait?

Q210855.t: A remote sea between Seram and New Guinea's Bird's Head
Q210855.s: The Ceram Sea stretches between the long, mountainous island of Seram and the western tip of New Guinea, known as the Bird's Head. On its northern side lie the limestone islands of Misool, part of Raja Ampat, where reefs hold some of the richest marine life on Earth. From above, look for jungle-clad ridges plunging straight into deep blue water.
Q210855.w: Deep-blue sea between the long green island of Seram and the western tip of New Guinea, with small limestone islands to the north.
f: Seram's highest mountain, Binaiya, rises to about 3,000 m.
“Ceram” is an old spelling of Seram, the island on its southern side.

q.q: What is the western tip of New Guinea, by the Ceram Sea, nicknamed?

Q639399.t: A remote Pacific gulf with record-breaking tides
Q639399.s: Shelikhov Gulf is the wild north-eastern corner of the Sea of Okhotsk, wedged between Kamchatka and the mainland. At its head, Penzhina Bay has the highest tides in the Pacific: the water can rise and fall by as much as 13 m, exposing vast mudflats. In winter the whole gulf is locked in drifting ice.
Q639399.w: A long gulf between Kamchatka's mountains and the mainland of Russia's Far East, white with ice in winter.
f: It is named after Grigory Shelikhov, the merchant who founded the first permanent Russian settlement in Alaska in 1784.
Penzhina Bay's tides are the highest anywhere in Russia.

q.q: Where are the highest tides in the Pacific Ocean?

Q163434.t: A shallow, ice-bound sea off Siberia's far north-east
Q163434.s: The East Siberian Sea stretches from the New Siberian Islands to Wrangel Island, and for most of the year it is a white, frozen plain. It is also remarkably shallow, mostly less than 50 m deep, and in summer the brown water of the Indigirka and Kolyma spreads across its surface. Pack ice often clings to the coast even in August.
Q163434.w: Ice or grey water off the low tundra coast of north-eastern Siberia, between the New Siberian Islands and Wrangel Island.
f: The Bear Islands, a small archipelago, lie off the mouth of the Kolyma.
The port of Pevek on its shore is often called Russia's northernmost town.

q.q: Which two rivers flow into the East Siberian Sea?

Q845217.t: A shallow Arctic basin with an island found from the air
Q845217.s: Foxe Basin is a shallow, ice-bound sea north of Hudson Bay, and its ice is sometimes tinged brown by sediment stirred up from the seafloor. It kept a secret for a long time: Prince Charles Island, roughly the size of Cyprus, was put on the map only in 1948, after it was spotted from an aircraft.
Q845217.w: A broad, shallow, often ice-covered sea west of Baffin Island, with low, flat islands in its eastern part.
f: It is named after Luke Foxe, who explored it in 1631.
Its shallow waters are a key home for Atlantic walruses.
Igloolik, an Inuit community, lies on an island at its north-western corner.

q.q: How was Prince Charles Island in Foxe Basin discovered in 1948?

Q509321.t: An iceberg-filled sea off East Antarctica
Q509321.s: The Davis Sea is a remote sea on the edge of East Antarctica, crowded with icebergs and fast ice for most of the year. Along its coast, the ice sheet ends in high white cliffs and the broad Shackleton Ice Shelf. On its shore stands Mirny, founded in 1956 as the first Soviet station in Antarctica.
Q509321.w: Pack ice and scattered icebergs along the edge of the East Antarctic ice sheet, which ends here in white ice cliffs.
f: It is named after John King Davis, captain of the Aurora on Douglas Mawson's 1911–14 expedition.
Mirny, on its shore, still serves as a Russian research station.

q.q: Which station, founded in 1956, stands on the Davis Sea?

Q7347.t: Five inland seas holding a fifth of Earth's fresh water
Q7347.s: From cruise height the Great Lakes look like seas, their far shores often lost in haze. Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie and Ontario form the largest group of freshwater lakes on Earth, holding about a fifth of the world's fresh surface water. In winter, cold air crossing them builds bands of cloud and dumps heavy lake-effect snow on their shores.
Q7347.w: Five huge interconnected lakes on the US–Canada border, from Superior in the west to Ontario in the east.
f: Water from Lake Superior drops about 100 m on its way to Lake Ontario, most of it along the Niagara River.
Together they hold about 84% of North America's fresh surface water.
Ships can sail from Lake Superior all the way to the Atlantic through locks and the St Lawrence Seaway.

q.q: Which of the Great Lakes is the largest by area?
